rulings.topic: No secret money: nothing is sent to either family without both knowing.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol I.3): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: No secret money: nothing is sent to either family without both knowing.

held_by.citation: Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol I.3

grounds.citation: A Christian Directory, Part II: Christian Oeconomicks, § 12
grounds.quote: if a Wife shall secretly waste or give, or lay it out on bravery, or vanity, or set her wit against her Husbands, and because she thinks him too strait or penurious, therefore she will dispose of it without his consent, this is thievery, disobedience and injustice
grounds.point: Secret giving out of the household's goods is condemned outright.

grounds.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife.
grounds.quote: That Common-wealth may in some sort be said to be happy, where they haue no vse of these words: Mine and thine; but in marriage especially they ought not to be heard
grounds.point: The goods of husband and wife are common, so neither keeps a separate secret store.

grounds.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife.
grounds.quote: The husband (as the head and chiefe guide of the family,) must haue the custody and chiese gouernment of the goods in the house
grounds.point: The common purse still has a governor: the husband.

grounds.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife.
grounds.quote: Yet let him remember, that he intreate her not as a seruant, by giuing her money as it were in mistrust, or with condition to returne him a particular account
grounds.point: His government of the purse must not become suspicion of his wife.

grounds.citation: A Christian Directory, § 23
grounds.quote: And as it is most dangerous for a man to be unknown to himself, so is it very hurtful to Husband or Wife, to be unknown to one another, in those cases wherein they have need of help
grounds.point: Husband and wife should not hide their affairs from one another.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 54 · Of husbands allowing their wiues to bestow on others, as they see good occasion.
grounds.quote: an husband should according to his ability let his wife haue some stocke, and portion of her owne, free to her selfe to dispose as she seeth good
grounds.point: Gouge allows the wife a portion she may give from at her own discretion, so not every gift needs both to agree.

grounds.citation: Proverbs 31:11
grounds.quote: The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil
grounds.point: Trust between them over the household's goods is the scriptural pattern.

rulings.revision: Keep no secret purse: the goods of the house are ours, not mine and thine, and nothing goes to either family behind the other's back; the husband governs the purse, but not in mistrust of his wife.
rulings.resolution: The manuals condemn secret giving out of the common goods: Baxter calls a wife's secret disposing against her husband's mind thievery, and Gouge names secret hoarding and selling behind a husband's back. Cleaver teaches that in marriage the goods are common ("this is ours"), with the husband holding the chief government of them but not dealing with his wife in mistrust. The protocol's symmetry (both must know) is a fair inference from the common goods and from Baxter's warning against being unknown to one another; what the sources add is that the husband governs the purse, and that he should leave his wife a portion of her own to give from.

rulings.topic: Once they marry, counsel when asked and let the new house govern itself.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol II): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Once they marry, counsel when asked and let the new house govern itself.

held_by.citation: Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol II

grounds.citation: Genesis 2:24
grounds.quote: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh
grounds.point: Marriage makes a new unit that the parents' house does not absorb.

grounds.citation: A Compleat Body of Divinity in Two Hundred and Fifty Expository Lectures on the , SERMON CLXXVII.
grounds.quote: WHEN they are Marrited, tho' they o〈…〉 a reverence to their Parents, yet they are 〈…〉 at their own dispose. They now set up 〈…〉 themselves, and make a distinct Family, whereof they have the charge upon them
grounds.point: Willard: the married couple heads a distinct family and is at its own disposal.

grounds.citation: A Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse touching the Honour due from Children to Paren, CHAP. III. Of Honour in speciall due to Parents, and that in a direct way, and therein of Honour of respect and love due to Parents.
grounds.quote: when you are called ... to maried conditions, then for Parents sakes, to neglect just respects to your spouses, and regard to your Families welfare
grounds.point: Cobbet counts it a fault to let a parent's wishes override a spouse and one's own household.

grounds.citation: Familiaris Consortio, 27 · The Elderly in the Family
grounds.quote: they continue to be present and to take an active and responsible part in family life, though having to respect the autonomy of the new family
grounds.point: The elders stay involved but respect the new household's autonomy.

grounds.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2230
grounds.quote: This necessary restraint does not prevent them - quite the contrary from giving their children judicious advice, particularly when they are planning to start a family
grounds.point: Parents' counsel is expected, not only given when asked.

grounds.citation: A Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse touching the Honour due from Children to Paren, CHAP. III. Of Honour in speciall due to Parents, and that in a direct way, and therein of Honour of respect and love due to Parents.
grounds.quote: how long did Jacobs Sons imploy themselves, in the Managing their Fathers estate and outward affaires & supplies? not alone before their Marriage
grounds.point: Married sons still served their father's affairs; the bond does not end at marriage.

rulings.revision: Once your children marry, let their house govern itself under its own head; give them sound counsel, and never come between husband and wife.
rulings.resolution: Willard teaches that married children, though they owe their parents reverence, are at their own disposal and "make a distinct Family"; Scripture's "leave his father and his mother" and Cobbet's warning not to neglect a spouse for a parent's sake support letting the new house govern itself. But the sources do not limit parents to counsel "when asked": the Catechism of the Catholic Church expects parents to give judicious advice, especially when the young are starting a family, and Familiaris Consortio speaks of the elderly as a "source of wisdom" who still respect "the autonomy of the new family." Cobbet also shows married sons still serving their father's affairs, so the bond of honor continues after marriage.

rulings.topic: Ask their advice before major decisions; if choosing otherwise, explain it to them with …
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol II.2-3): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Ask their advice before major decisions; if choosing otherwise, explain it to them with honor.

held_by.citation: Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol II.2-3

grounds.citation: A Compleat Body of Divinity in Two Hundred and Fifty Expository Lectures on the , SERMON CLXXVII.
grounds.quote: Doubtless when they come to be for themselve, they have a liberty to use their own Prudence in ordering their Affairs, tho' with a due deference to the Advice of their Parents
grounds.point: Grown children decide for themselves, but with due deference to their parents' advice.

grounds.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2230
grounds.quote: They should assume their new responsibilities within a trusting relationship with their parents, willingly asking and receiving their advice and counsel
grounds.point: Adult children should seek out their parents' counsel.

grounds.citation: Casti Connubii, 115
grounds.quote: let them not omit to ask the prudent advice of their parents with regard to the partner, and let them regard this advice in no light manner
grounds.point: Above all for marriage, the parents' advice is to be sought and weighed.

grounds.citation: A Christian Directory, § 6
grounds.quote: Parents have no authority to command you any thing against God or your salvation or your
grounds.point: Choosing otherwise is lawful where obeying would go against God.

grounds.citation: A Christian Directory, § 10
grounds.quote: But if they would force you to joyn your selves to such as are ungodly, and like to make your lives either sinful or miserable, you may humbly refuse them
grounds.point: Even a lawful refusal is made humbly.

rulings.revision: Once grown, ask your parents' advice before the great decisions of your life and weigh it with deference; if conscience or prudence leads you another way, tell them humbly and with honor.
rulings.resolution: Willard writes that children who are "for themselves" may order their own affairs, "tho' with a due deference to the Advice of their Parents"; the Catechism of the Catholic Church asks adult children to be "willingly asking and receiving their advice and counsel," and Casti Connubii asks the same about choosing a spouse. Baxter and Gouge set the limit: parents have no authority to command against God, and a child may then humbly refuse. The protocol stands; the revision only names the deference and humility the sources require.

rulings.topic: Send the regular gift to parents, agreed between husband and wife.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol I.2): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Send the regular gift to parents, agreed between husband and wife.

held_by.citation: Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol I.2

grounds.citation: 1 Timothy 5:4
grounds.quote: let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God
grounds.point: Children owe their parents a return.

grounds.quote: If a man shall say to his father or mother, [It is] Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; [he shall be free]. And ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother
grounds.point: Christ condemns any excuse for withholding support from parents.

grounds.citation: A Christian Directory, § 11
grounds.quote: If your Parents be in want, it is your duty to relieve them according to your ability
grounds.point: The measure is the parents' want and the child's ability.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Of childrens releeuing their parents according to their neede.
grounds.quote: Contrary also is their practise, who hauing the goods of this world, suffer their parents to want
grounds.point: Gouge condemns children of means who let their parents go short.

grounds.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife.
grounds.quote: so each alike shall vndertake the custody and employment of the same
grounds.point: Husband and wife share the care of how the common goods are used.

rulings.revision: Relieve your parents according to their need and your ability, and maintain them wholly if they need it; husband and wife settle together what is given.
rulings.resolution: The duty to support parents is among the best attested in the library: Scripture tells children to "requite their parents," Christ condemns the Corban evasion, and Baxter and Gouge make it a duty to relieve parents in want and even to maintain them wholly. But the sources measure it by the parents' need and the child's ability, not by a fixed regular gift; a gift made out of plenty is honorable, but it is not what the sources command. That husband and wife agree on it follows from the common goods of marriage (see the ruling on secret money).

rulings.topic: Marry with your parents' knowledge and blessing sought, not behind their backs.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Our house): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Marry with your parents' knowledge and blessing sought, not behind their backs.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Throughout the Three Kingdoms of En, The Solemnization of Marriage.
grounds.quote: The like is to be observed in the proceedings of all others, although of age, whose Parents are living, for their first marriage
grounds.point: Westminster requires the parents' consent for a first marriage even when the child is of age: more than "blessing sought."

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Throughout the Three Kingdoms of En, The Solemnization of Marriage.
grounds.quote: And in after marriages of either of those parties, they shall be exhorted not to contract marriage, without first acquainting their Parents with it, (if with conveniency it may be done) endevouring to obtaine their consent
grounds.point: For later marriages, telling the parents and seeking their consent is the rule.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Throughout the Three Kingdoms of En, The Solemnization of Marriage.
grounds.quote: Parents ought not to force their children to marry without their free consent, nor deny their own consent without just cause
grounds.point: The parents' power is bounded: no forcing, no refusal without cause.

grounds.citation: The Whole Duty of Man, Partitions XIV-XV: Of Duty to Parents and of Parents to C, § 14 — Obedience … § 17 — Duty to be paid even to the worst Parents
grounds.quote: that of marrying against the consent of the Parent, is one of the highest
grounds.point: The Whole Duty of Man counts marrying against a parent's consent among the gravest disobediences.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Of parents consent to the mariage of their children.
grounds.quote: The ancient fathers of the Church haue in their ages taught children this duty, and pronounced mariages of children without consent of parents, to be vnlawfull
grounds.point: Gouge treats consent, not mere knowledge, as the duty.

grounds.citation: A Christian Directory, § 10
grounds.quote: But if they would force you to joyn your selves to such as are ungodly, and like to make your lives either sinful or miserable, you may humbly refuse them
grounds.point: The child may humbly refuse an ungodly match.

rulings.revision: Do not marry without your parents' consent; for a first marriage have it even when you are of age, and for a later one tell them first and seek it. Parents must neither force a match nor refuse consent without just cause.
rulings.resolution: The protocol asks too little. The Westminster Directory requires that the parents' consent be made known to the church officers before a first marriage, even for those of age, and for later marriages that the parties acquaint their parents and endeavor to obtain their consent; Gouge, The Whole Duty of Man and the Massachusetts laws treat marrying without consent as a grave wrong. The same Directory binds the parents: they may not force a child to marry or deny consent without just cause, and Baxter allows a child to refuse an ungodly match humbly.

rulings.topic: Share the care of parents; do not leave it to one.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Our house): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Share the care of parents; do not leave it to one.

grounds.citation: The Whole Duty of Man, Partitions XIV-XV: Of Duty to Parents and of Parents to C, § 14 — Obedience … § 17 — Duty to be paid even to the worst Parents
grounds.quote: in all these the child is bound according to his ability
grounds.point: The duty rests on each child, measured by ability.

grounds.citation: Provincial poor-law extracts: Massachusetts Bay 1692-3 ch. 28 ss. 8-10 and New H, [Sect. 8.] … [Sect. 10.]
grounds.quote: then such relations respectively shall relieve such poor person in such manner as the justices of the peace in that county where such sufficient persons dwell shall assess, on pain that every one failing therein shall forfeit twenty shillings for every month's neglect
grounds.point: Massachusetts law held each able relation to his share.

grounds.citation: An Act for the Relief of the Poor, 43 Eliz. I c. 2, V. … XI.
grounds.quote: being of a sufficient Ability, shall at their own Charges relieve and maintain every such poor Person in that Manner, and according to that Rate, as by the Justices of Peace
grounds.point: The English poor law of 1601 apportioned the burden among the able kin.

grounds.citation: A Christian Directory, § 11
grounds.quote: If your Parents be in want, it is your duty to relieve them according to your ability: [marg.: Direct. 11.] yea, and wholly to maintain them if there be need
grounds.point: Baxter: the duty runs to whole maintenance if needed.

rulings.revision: Share the care of your parents among you, each according to his ability; do not leave it all to one.
rulings.resolution: Every source that speaks of it lays the duty on each child according to his ability: The Whole Duty of Man ("the child is bound according to his ability"), Baxter, and the English and Massachusetts poor laws, which assess each relation of sufficient ability to relieve parents and grandparents and fine every one who fails. Leaving the whole burden to one child breaks that duty for the others. The revision adds the measure, ability, that the sources give.

rulings.topic: Give your parents real time with their grandchildren, in person or by call.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol III.3): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Give your parents real time with their grandchildren, in person or by call.

held_by.citation: Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol III.3

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 4:9
grounds.quote: but teach them thy sons, and thy sons’ sons
grounds.point: The older generation is charged to teach its grandchildren.

grounds.citation: Genesis 48:9
grounds.quote: And Joseph said unto his father, They [are] my sons, whom God hath given me in this place. And he said, Bring them, I pray thee, unto me, and I will bless them
grounds.point: The father brings his sons to their grandfather.

grounds.citation: 2 Timothy 1:5
grounds.quote: the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice
grounds.point: Faith passed from grandmother to grandchild.

grounds.citation: Proverbs 17:6
grounds.quote: Children’s children [are] the crown of old men
grounds.point: Grandchildren are the honor of the old.

grounds.citation: Familiaris Consortio, 27 · The Elderly in the Family
grounds.quote: above all they carry out the important mission of being a witness to the past and a source of wisdom for the young and for the future
grounds.point: The elderly have a role toward the young of the family.

rulings.revision: Bring your children to their grandparents, so that the old may know them, teach them and bless them.
rulings.resolution: Scripture gives grandparents a part in the grandchildren's raising: Moses commands "teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons," Joseph brings his sons to Jacob to be blessed, and Paul traces Timothy's faith to his grandmother Lois. Familiaris Consortio describes the elderly as "a source of wisdom for the young." The sources support the protocol and give its purpose; the revision names that purpose. A call is a modern means to the same end.

rulings.topic: Stand in front: take criticism aimed at his wife or children upon himself.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol III.2): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Stand in front: take criticism aimed at his wife or children upon himself.

held_by.citation: Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol III.2

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 58 · Of an husbands protecting his wife from danger.
grounds.quote: In regard of that protection which an husband oweth his wife, he is called the veile of her eies
grounds.point: The husband covers and protects his wife.

grounds.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife.
grounds.quote: yet he may not abuse or despise her, but most louingly defend and keepe her from all iniuries, and all euils as his owne body
grounds.point: He defends her from every injury as his own body.

grounds.citation: A Christian Directory, § 5
grounds.quote: Children or Servants must not be suffered to carry themselves contemptuously or rudely towards them, nor to despise them, or speak unmannerly, proud or disdainful words to them. The Husband must vindicate them from all such injury and contempt
grounds.point: He stands between his wife and contempt.

grounds.citation: Oeconomicus, Chapter 3
grounds.quote: If it goes ill with the sheep we blame the shepherd, as a rule, or if a horse shows vice we throw the blame in general upon the rider
grounds.point: Xenophon: the blame for a household's faults falls on the one who leads it.

grounds.citation: A Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse touching the Honour due from Children to Paren, CHAP. VII. Of Honour in a Reflect way due from Children unto Parents.
grounds.quote: as it is in the case of Elders of Churches, its put upon their account of blame, if their Children be accused of Riot, or are unruly
grounds.point: Cobbet: children's disorder is laid to the father's account.

grounds.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife.
grounds.quote: albeit the wife should minister iust cause of griefe and displeasure, yet that the husband should not thereof take occasion against his wiues infirmities; or enter into bitternesse, taunts, or disquietnesse: but discreetly, and patiently beare with her
grounds.point: He bears with her faults patiently rather than exposing them.

rulings.revision: Defend your wife and children from others' injury and contempt, and answer for your house yourself, since its faults are laid at your door.
rulings.resolution: The manuals make the husband his wife's protector: Gouge calls him "the veile of her eies," Cleaver says he must "most louingly defend" her, and Baxter says he "must vindicate them from all such injury and contempt." Xenophon and Cobbet add that the faults of a household are laid to its head. The protocol's picture of the head standing in front is supported; the sources speak of defending and answering, not of absorbing every criticism, and the same manuals keep the head's duty to reprove his household privately when it is at fault.

rulings.topic: See that no young man or woman of the family is left without help toward marriage.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Our house): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: See that no young man or woman of the family is left without help toward marriage.

grounds.citation: Rules of the Fan Lineage Charitable Estate (范氏義莊規矩)
grounds.quote: 嫁女支錢三十貫〈七十七陌下並准此〉再嫁二十貫
grounds.point: The clan estate pays thirty strings of cash toward each daughter's marriage.

grounds.citation: Rules of the Fan Lineage Charitable Estate (范氏義莊規矩)
grounds.quote: 娶婦支錢二十貫再娶不支
grounds.point: And twenty toward each son's first marriage.

grounds.citation: Yi I (Yulgok), Village Compact (鄕約), mutual aid
grounds.quote: 年壯處女貧甚。過時未嫁者。報官給資裝。約中亦隨宜扶助。
grounds.point: A poor woman past the age of marrying is helped with a trousseau by the compact.

grounds.citation: Yi I (Yulgok), Village Compact (鄕約), the orphaned and weak
grounds.quote: 若其子稍長。則擇人敎之。且爲求婚姻。
grounds.point: For the orphans of members, the compact finds them teachers and seeks marriages for them.

grounds.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife.
grounds.quote: Now by parents we vnderstand not onely the naturall parents, but such as by the law of nature and of God, supply their places: as grandfathers, great grand-fathers, vncles, aunts, great vncles and aunts, brethren, sisters, kins-men, and kins-women
grounds.point: Kin stand in the place of parents in seeing the young married.

grounds.citation: A Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse touching the Honour due from Children to Paren, CHAP. VII. Of Honour in a Reflect way due from Children unto Parents.
grounds.quote: Hence the Apostles counsell to Parents, to dispose seasonably of their Virgins in marriage, 1 Cor. 7. 36
grounds.point: Seeing the young married in season is a charge on their elders.

rulings.resolution: Clan provision for marriage is directly attested. The Fan lineage charitable estate paid money toward every daughter's marriage and every son's wedding, and Yulgok's village compact provided for a poor woman past the age of marrying and sought marriages for the clan's orphans. Cleaver counts uncles, aunts and kinsmen among the "parents" who stand in for the dead in matching the young, and Cobbet reads 1 Corinthians 7:36 as a charge to dispose of the young in marriage in season.

rulings.topic: On the anniversaries of our dead, tell their stories (remembrance, not jesa).
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Covenant Home: Tradition and Culture II): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: On the anniversaries of our dead, tell their stories (remembrance, not jesa).

held_by.citation: Covenant Home: Tradition and Culture II

grounds.citation: Proverbs 10:7
grounds.quote: The memory of the just [is] blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot
grounds.point: Keeping the memory of the righteous is blessed.

grounds.citation: Hebrews 13:7
grounds.quote: Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of [their] conversation
grounds.point: Remember the faithful dead and follow their faith.

grounds.citation: A Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse touching the Honour due from Children to Paren, CHAP. VII. Of Honour in a Reflect way due from Children unto Parents.
grounds.quote: and to maintain their names, even when they are dead, all they can
grounds.point: Children keep their parents' names after death.

grounds.citation: Records of the China Centenary Missionary Conference, Shanghai 1907, Resolution I (p. 623)
grounds.quote: yet we should be careful to encourage in our Christian converts, the feeling of reverence for the memory of the departed which this custom seeks to express
grounds.point: The conference that rejected ancestral worship kept reverence for the memory of the dead.

grounds.citation: Judges 11:39–40
grounds.quote: And it was a custom in Israel, [That] the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year
grounds.point: Scripture records a yearly remembrance of the dead, as a custom and not a command.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, An Appendix touching Dayes and Places for Publique worship.
grounds.quote: Festivall daies, vulgarly called Holy daies, having no warrant in the word of God, are not to be continued
grounds.point: A fixed day must not become a holy day.

rulings.revision: Keep the memory and good name of our dead: tell their faith and their stories to the generations after, and make no rite or holy day of it.
rulings.resolution: Remembrance is well grounded: "the memory of the just is blessed," "remember them which have the rule over you... whose faith follow," and Cobbet's duty to maintain parents' names "even when they are dead." The 1907 Shanghai Conference, in rejecting ancestral worship, urged Christians to keep "an affectionate remembrance of the dead." Fixing it to the anniversary is the drafter's addition: Scripture records yearly remembrances (Jephthah's daughter, the lamentations for Josiah) without commanding them, the death-day is the very day of jesa, and the Westminster Directory allows no holy days without warrant. An anniversary may serve as an occasion, but not as a rite.

rulings.topic: Stay reachable: answer the family, and do not go silent for seasons.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Our house): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Stay reachable: answer the family, and do not go silent for seasons.

grounds.citation: Proverbs 27:10
grounds.quote: Thine own friend, and thy father’s friend, forsake not
grounds.point: Do not drop the bonds you inherit.

grounds.citation: A Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse touching the Honour due from Children to Paren, CHAP. III. Of Honour in speciall due to Parents, and that in a direct way, and therein of Honour of respect and love due to Parents.
grounds.quote: but especially they are to cleave to Brethren and Sisters of the same Parents
grounds.point: Above all, keep close to brothers and sisters.

grounds.citation: Khü Lî, Qu Li I.ii.5
grounds.quote: A son, when he is going abroad, must inform (his parents where he is going); when he returns, he must present himself before them
grounds.point: A child keeps his parents informed of where he is.

rulings.revision: Do not forsake your kin: let your parents know where you are, and keep up your bond with your brothers and sisters and your father's friends.
rulings.resolution: Scripture says "thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not," and Cobbet adds that children must "especially" cleave to their brothers and sisters. The Book of Rites tells a son to inform his parents where he is going and to present himself when he returns (Confucian, low weight). These support the protocol's substance. "Answer the family" and "seasons" are the drafter's words for it; the sources speak of not forsaking kin, not of a duty to be on call.

rulings.topic: Loyalty: take the family's side in public and bring grievances to the family in private.
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Our house): does the literature support it?
rulings.practice: Loyalty: take the family's side in public and bring grievances to the family in private.

grounds.citation: Matthew 18:15
grounds.quote: Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother
grounds.point: Grievances go first to the one concerned, in private.

grounds.citation: 1 Corinthians 6:6–7
grounds.quote: But brother goeth to law with brother, and that before the unbelievers. Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you
grounds.point: Quarrels among kin should not be taken before outsiders.

grounds.citation: Proverbs 25:9
grounds.quote: Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another
grounds.point: Settle it with the person; do not spread it.

grounds.citation: The Whole Duty of Man, Partitions XIV-XV: Of Duty to Parents and of Parents to C, § 11 — Duties to our natural Parents
grounds.quote: it must be our business to cover, and conceal them; like Shem, and Japhet, who while cursed Cham publisht and disclosed the nakedness of their father, covered it
grounds.point: Cover a parent's infirmities rather than publish them.

grounds.citation: Exodus 23:2
grounds.quote: Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest
grounds.point: Taking a side never extends to joining in wrong.

grounds.citation: A Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse touching the Honour due from Children to Paren, CHAP. III. Of Honour in speciall due to Parents, and that in a direct way, and therein of Honour of respect and love due to Parents.

rulings.revision: Bring a grievance against kin to them privately first and settle family quarrels within the family, not before outsiders; cover their infirmities, but never side with them in sin or against the truth.
rulings.resolution: The private half is well grounded: Christ's rule to tell a brother "his fault between thee and him alone," Paul's rebuke of "brother goeth to law with brother... before the unbelievers," Proverbs' charge to debate a cause with the man himself and not discover it to another, and The Whole Duty of Man's charge to cover parents' infirmities as Shem and Japheth did. The public half, taking the family's side, the sources limit: "thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil," and Cobbet requires children to bear witness against a parent's sin when God calls for it. Loyalty is owed in covering faults and in keeping quarrels in the family, not in defending wrong.

grounds.point: The new wife was taught the ways of the house by her husband.

rulings.resolution: The household head's duty to teach those who come into the house is attested across the traditions. Scripture gathers "thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn," and Abraham commands "his household after him." The Book of Common Prayer charges masters and dames to bring servants and apprentices to be taught, and Xenophon's Ischomachus teaches his young wife the ordering of the house himself. Patience in teaching is Paul's "in meekness instructing" and Cleaver's "discreetly, and patiently."

rulings.topic: At a funeral, bow to the mourners and comfort them; stand in silence before the dead rat…
rulings.question: Our house protocol (Our house): does the literature support it?

grounds.quote: but it does not in itself form an act of idolatry, because the same posture is employed to show respect to the living
grounds.point: Martin, pleading for toleration, held that the posture is not idolatry in itself, since it is also used to the living.

grounds.citation: Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China, Shanghai 1890: H. Blodget, "The Attitude of Christianity toward Ancestral Worship" (pp. 631-654)
grounds.quote: There is implied in all that pertains to it an intercommunication between the living and the dead, which is foreign to the tenets of Christianity
grounds.point: Blodget's answer: whatever the posture, the rites imply speaking with the dead, which Christianity does not allow.

grounds.citation: Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China, Shanghai 1890, Resolution VII (p. lxiv)
grounds.quote: Resolved. That this Conference record its dissent from this conclusion and affirm its belief that idolatry is an essential constituent of ancestral worship.
grounds.point: The Conference formally rejected Martin's plea for toleration.

grounds.citation: Ecclesiastes 9:5
grounds.quote: For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing
grounds.point: The dead do not receive the honor that a bow presents.

grounds.citation: Genesis 23:5–7
grounds.quote: And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land, [even] to the children of Heth
grounds.point: At Sarah's burial Abraham bowed to the living.

grounds.citation: Romans 12:15
grounds.quote: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep
grounds.point: The duty at a funeral is toward the mourners.

grounds.citation: Plane compertum est: Instructio circa quasdam caeremonias et iuramentum super ri, (opening)
grounds.quote: and holds bows and other civil observances before the dead, their images and name-tablets to be lawful
grounds.point: The 1939 Catholic instruction permits bows before the dead as civil acts.

grounds.citation: Records of the China Centenary Missionary Conference, Shanghai 1907, committee report, "Prostration" (p. 219)
grounds.quote: and though we may object to it as a matter of custom, let us not make such things a matter of conscience
grounds.point: The 1907 committee urged that prostrations not be made a matter of conscience.

rulings.resolution: The protocol draws the line where the Westminster Directory draws it: kneeling and praying "by, or towards the dead Corps" are superstitious, but "civill respects" at the burial remain. At the 1890 Shanghai Conference, W. A. P. Martin argued that the posture is not idolatry in itself, since the same bow is made to the living. The Conference formally dissented from his plea, and Blodget's paper gave the reason: the rites imply "an intercommunication between the living and the dead," and "the dead know not any thing." The bow, then, is not wrong in itself, but a bow made to the dead treats them as present to receive it. Abraham at Sarah's burial bowed to the living, and Scripture bids us weep with the mourners. Against the protocol stand Martin and the 1939 Catholic instruction, which hold bows before the dead to be lawful civil acts, and the 1907 committee's plea not to make prostrations a matter of conscience. All three rank below Scripture and Westminster here.

rulings.allowed: One husband and one wife for life. A childless couple stays faithful to each other; a wife's lack of a son is never a reason to bring another woman into the marriage.
rulings.resolution: God joined one man to one wife as one flesh, and the Westminster standards call having more wives than one at the same time a sin against the seventh commandment, whatever the need for heirs. The patriarchs' concubines are no warrant: Gouge calls them 'their sinne', and Sarah and Hagar show the grief that rivalry brings. So no man of our house takes a concubine or second wife, and no wife is told to bear one without jealousy, much less to procure one. The rite that presents a woman as one of 'the providers of sons' treats her as a means to the line and is set aside.

rulings.allowed: Record every child under his own father and his own mother, plainly and truthfully. Children owe their father's wife the honor of a mother, and half-brothers deal with each other as brothers.
rulings.resolution: The law of Moses forbids a father to rank his sons by his regard for their mothers, and Scripture counts the handmaids' sons among 'the sons of Jacob'. No child bears the iniquity of his parents, and in Christ there is 'neither bond nor free'. Abraham's gifts to the sons of his concubines followed God's particular word that 'in Isaac shall thy seed be called', a promise about the covenant line and not a rule of rank, and even there God said of Ishmael 'he is thy seed'. Our house takes no concubines, so this ruling governs how earlier generations are written in our records and how any child born outside marriage is received: no child is entered with a 'lower status', denied the name of son, or ranked below his brothers in honor or mourning because of his mother.

Gouge says plainly that keeping a married child from husband or wife is 'more then a parents authority reacheth vnto', that a spouse is to be preferred before parents, and that the time to weigh a match is before the marriage, for 'After mariage it is too late to seeke such a redresse.' rulings.resolution: The Westminster standards say nothing about contraception or periodic continence. They name procreation as one of three ends of marriage, alongside mutual help and the prevention of uncleanness. What our sources do say is weighty, and we keep it: children are a heritage of the LORD; husband and wife may abstain only by consent and for a time; and Gouge, reading Onan, calls refusing the marriage duty worse when it springs from 'feare of hauing too many children'. Rome reads Onan as condemning every act that prevents conception; Scripture states his sin as acting 'lest that he should give seed to his brother', and our standards draw no rule about means from it. So we set aside the Roman rule as Church law over the conscience (WCF 20.2): the house neither forbids by law what our standards leave unaddressed nor makes periodic continence the one approved method, which Gouge's warning, if anything, tells against when it is used to avoid children.

rulings.resolution: Our standards command what is right in this practice: the infants of believing parents are to be baptized, and parents promise to bring them up in the knowledge of the Christian religion. But baptism does not regenerate by being given ('not so inseparably annexed'), there are only two sacraments, so penance and the rest are no sacraments of the gospel, and the Mass is 'most abominably injurious to Christs one, only Sacrifice'. Devotion and consecration to the Sacred Heart is worship devised by men and not prescribed in Scripture. So we set aside raising children through the Roman sacraments, devotions and church-controlled schooling, and keep baptism and Christian nurture in the Reformed way.

grounds.quote: 終喪不入妻室，稍知義理，不待防閑之嚴，而自不忍爲矣
grounds.point: The Sangbyeon Tonggo commends never entering the wife's room for the whole mourning period.

rulings.allowed: Husband and wife abstain during the wife's monthly period, as Leviticus 18:19 and the Puritans teach, and may abstain by mutual consent for a season of fasting and prayer. In grief they comfort each other.
rulings.resolution: Two parts of this practice stand on our sources and are kept: abstinence during the wife's period, which Leviticus forbids and Gouge and Perkins teach, and abstinence by consent 'for a time' for fasting and prayer. Mandatory abstinence for the whole mourning period or for calendar vigils has no ground in Scripture. David 'comforted Bath-sheba his wife, and went in unto her' after their child died, Paul allows abstinence only by consent and for a time, no one may judge us 'in respect of an holyday', and Gouge will not 'make that a sinne which is not there condemned'. Those rules are set aside.

rulings.topic: Wives blamed for discord among brothers
rulings.question: Do we treat a wife's counsel as a danger to brotherly unity and put brothers above wife and children?
rulings.practice: Do not let your wife's words divide you from your brothers: keep the property undivided, relieve your brother even against her wishes, and hold your brothers dearer than wife and children.

held_by.quote: 外與兄弟相愛常不失歡，私救其所急，私周其所乏 — Outwardly love your brothers without losing harmony; secretly relieve their urgent needs and supply their wants.
But brothers more than they Can satisfy the heart. 'Tis their accord does peace afford

held_by.citation: Sohak Eonhae, Outer Part: Admirable Sayings and Good Conduct, 嘉言 49
held_by.quote: 男子剛腸者幾人, 能不爲婦人言所或 — How many men have strong enough character not to be deluded by women's words?
兄弟四人, 皆同財業. 及各取妻, 諸婦遂求分異, 又數有鬪爭之言 — Four brothers shared property; after each took a wife, the women sought division and quarreled.
諸婦遂求分異, 又數有鬪爭之言 — The wives sought division and had frequent quarreling words.

held_by.citation: Sohak Eonhae, Outer Part: Admirable Sayings and Good Conduct, 嘉言 49
held_by.quote: 人家兄弟, 無不義者, 盡因娶婦入門... 皆汝婦人所作 — Brothers become unrighteous because wives enter the home; all this is done by you women.

grounds.citation: Genesis 2:24
grounds.quote: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
grounds.point: The wife is joined to her husband more closely than any kin.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Of the neere coniunction of man and wife together.
grounds.quote: The neerest of all other are husband and wife one to another.
grounds.point: Gouge: no tie, brother's included, is nearer than husband and wife.

grounds.citation: 1 Timothy 5:8
grounds.quote: But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
grounds.point: A man's first duty of provision is to his own household.

grounds.citation: Psalms 133:1
grounds.quote: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
grounds.point: Brotherly unity is a good to be kept.

grounds.citation: 1 John 3:17
grounds.quote: But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?
grounds.point: Relieving a brother in need is a duty.

grounds.citation: Proverbs 6:19
grounds.quote: A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren.
grounds.point: Sowing discord among brothers is hateful to God, whoever does it.

grounds.citation: Acts 5:4
grounds.quote: Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power?
grounds.point: Holding property in common is voluntary, not a duty imposed.

grounds.citation: The State Of Equilibrium And Harmony, Zhong Yong I.42
grounds.quote: But brothers more than they Can satisfy the heart.
grounds.point: The Zhong Yong's ode ranks brothers above wife and children.

rulings.allowed: Keep peace among brothers, relieve a brother in need, and refuse slander and talebearing from anyone, wife or kinsman. Husband and wife settle their giving together.
rulings.resolution: Scripture does praise brothers who dwell together in unity, does require relief of a brother in need, and does condemn whoever 'soweth discord among brethren'; we keep all of that. But it puts the wife nearest: a man cleaves to his wife, Gouge calls husband and wife 'the neerest of all other', and he who does not provide for his own house 'hath denied the faith'. So we set aside ranking brothers above wife and children, treating a wife's counsel as a danger in itself, and requiring that property stay undivided. Property, Peter says, was 'thine own' while it remained.

rulings.topic: The same-surname marriage ban and kin degrees beyond Leviticus
rulings.question: Do we forbid marriage between people of the same surname and ancestral seat, or to the eighth degree of patrilineal kin?
rulings.practice: Do not marry anyone of your own surname and ancestral seat, however distant, nor anyone within eight degrees on the father's side.

held_by.quote: One must not marry a wife of the same surname with himself.
there could be no intermarriage, even after a hundred generations

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 동성동본불혼 현황
held_by.quote: 동성동본인 혈족 사이에서는 혼인하지 못한다 — Marriage is forbidden between blood relatives of the same surname and ancestral seat.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture, 친족 · 내용
held_by.quote: 규범상 동성동본 관계에 있는 이들은 서로 혼인할 수 없다 — By norm, those of the same surname and origin cannot marry each other.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture, 촌수 寸數 · 촌수 · 내용
held_by.quote: 동성동본의 부계친족을 ‘혈연관계’로 확대 해석하여 혼인을 금하는 관례는 19세기에나 일반화되기 시작하였다. — The custom of prohibiting marriage between patrilineal kin of the same surname and origin became common only in the 19th century.
鄕貫雖異, 姓字若同, 則毋得婚娶 — Though the clan seat differ, if the surname is the same, you must not marry.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture, 촌수 寸數 · 촌수 · 내용
held_by.quote: 근대법적으로 ‘친족’은 혈연관계에 근거하여 친가 8촌과 외가 4촌까지의 범위로 규정되고, 친족 내에서는 서로 혼인할 수 없다. — By modern law, kin were defined as up to 8 degrees on the father's side and 4 degrees on the mother's side, and marriage within kin was prohibited.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 친족 親族 · 친족 · 친족제도
held_by.quote: 조선시대에 와서는 동성불혼(同姓不婚)이라는 특징... 실제로는 동성동본불혼만 지켜졌을 뿐 — In Joseon, same-surname marriage was prohibited... actually only same-surname same-origin marriage was avoided.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 동성동본불혼 同姓同本不婚 … 연원 및 변천

grounds.citation: Leviticus 18:5–6
grounds.quote: None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.
grounds.point: God forbids marriage to near kin, and Leviticus 18 sets out who they are.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 24.4
grounds.quote: Marriage ought not to be within the degrees of Consanguinity or Affinity forbidden in the Word
grounds.point: The Confession binds us to the degrees forbidden in Scripture, not to further ones.

grounds.citation: Numbers 36:10–11
grounds.quote: the daughters of Zelophehad, were married unto their father's brothers' sons
grounds.point: Scripture records first cousins of the same paternal line marrying at God's direction.

grounds.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book I, chapters 14-17, I.
grounds.quote: nothing (God's law except) shall impeach any marriage, but within the Levitical degrees; the farthest of which is that between uncle and niece
grounds.point: English law limits impediments of kinship to the Levitical degrees.

grounds.citation: The Larger Catechism, WLC 139
grounds.quote: prohibiting of lawfull ... and dispensing with unlawfull marriages
grounds.point: Forbidding lawful marriages is a sin.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 20.2
grounds.quote: God alone is Lord of the Conscience, and hath left it free from the Doctrines and Commandments of men, which are, in any thing contrary to his Word; or beside it
grounds.point: Impediments beyond the Word do not bind the conscience.

grounds.citation: The Great Treatise, Da Zhuan 8
grounds.quote: there could be no intermarriage, even after a hundred generations.
grounds.point: The Liji forbids intermarriage under one surname without limit of generations.

grounds.citation: Khü Lî, Qu Li I.iii.38
grounds.quote: one must not marry a wife of the same surname with himself.
grounds.point: The Liji forbids marrying anyone of the same surname.

rulings.allowed: Keep the degrees forbidden in Leviticus 18 as the Westminster Confession reads them, affinity included, and check the family records so that no one marries within them. Beyond those degrees, sharing a surname and ancestral seat is no bar to marriage.
rulings.resolution: Scripture forbids marriage to 'any that is near of kin', and the Westminster Confession and Directory forbid the degrees 'forbidden in the Word'; we keep those. The same-surname ban reaches far beyond them, 'even after a hundred generations'. Scripture does not: the daughters of Zelophehad married their father's brothers' sons at God's command. English law, after the Reformation, held that nothing 'but within the Levitical degrees' impeaches a marriage. Adding impediments God did not make is 'prohibiting of lawfull' marriages and binds the conscience by commandments of men, so the surname-and-seat ban and the eight-degree rule are set aside.

rulings.topic: Parents choosing their children's spouses
rulings.question: How far may parents of our house arrange, compel, or forbid their children's marriages?
rulings.practice: Accept the marriage your parents arrange, see your daughter married by twenty, and do not obstinately refuse the one to whom you were betrothed, even in the cradle.

held_by.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
held_by.quote: the church held that the parents of the espoused girl might give her to another man, if she obstinately refused the man to whom she had been betrothed.

held_by.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Bk. II, ch.7 §1
held_by.quote: babies in the cradle were not to be given in marriage, except under the pressure of some urgent need, such as the desire for peace

held_by.citation: Sangbyeon Tonggo, Capping and Marriage Rites, 常變通攷 卷五 · 笄 · 笄 · 許嫁笄 … 乃禮賓
held_by.quote: 嫁止於二十，以其二十而不嫁，則爲非禮 — Marriage is limited to twenty; if at twenty she is not married, it is improper.

held_by.citation: Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse, CHAP. II
held_by.quote: cross matching against their minds

grounds.citation: Genesis 24:57–58
grounds.quote: We will call the damsel, and enquire at her mouth. And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go.
grounds.point: Even a match her family approved waited on Rebekah's own consent.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Throughout the Three Kingdoms of En, The Solemnization of Marriage.
grounds.quote: Parents ought not to force their children to marry without their free consent, nor deny their own consent without just cause.
grounds.point: The Directory forbids forced marriage and causeless refusal of consent alike.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Throughout the Three Kingdoms of En, The Solemnization of Marriage.
grounds.quote: The like is to be observed in the proceedings of all others, although of age, whose Parents are living, for their first marriage.
grounds.point: The Directory requires parents' consent for a first marriage, even for children of age.

grounds.citation: The Second Helvetic Confession, chapters IV, V, XXVI and XXIX, Second Helvetic Confession 29
grounds.quote: Let marriages be made with consent of the parents, or such as are instead of parents
grounds.point: The Second Helvetic Confession requires parents' consent.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 20 · Of obiections for childrens marrying without parents consent, answered.
grounds.quote: a childe therefore may no more marry for himselfe without consent of parents, then alienate his parents goods for himselfe.
grounds.point: Gouge makes parents' consent binding on the child.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 54 · Direction to parents in prouiding mariages.
grounds.quote: though the authority of parents ought in this case to be inuiolable, yet a middle course is so to be held, as the parties may willingly with a mutuall consent ioyne themselues together.
grounds.point: Gouge balances parents' authority with the couple's free mutual consent.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 24.3
grounds.quote: It is lawful for all sorts of people to marry, who are able with judgement, to give their Consent.
grounds.point: Marriage requires parties able to give consent, which infants cannot.

grounds.citation: The Larger Catechism, WLC 139
grounds.quote: intangling vows of single life ... undue delay of marriage
grounds.point: Undue delay of marriage is a sin, so parents rightly see their children married in good time.

rulings.allowed: Parents take real care to provide fit matches, children do not contract a first marriage without their parents' consent, and parents do not deny consent without just cause. Children are not left unmarried through neglect.
rulings.resolution: Our standards give parents real authority over a first marriage, and we keep it: the Directory requires parents' consent for a first marriage even of children of age, the Second Helvetic Confession says the same, and Gouge holds that a child may no more marry without consent than alienate his parents' goods. But the same Directory forbids parents to 'force their children to marry without their free consent', Rebekah was asked 'Wilt thou go with this man?', and Gouge would have parents use only 'faire meanes' and never force. Since the Confession requires persons able to give their own consent, betrothing infants is set aside. So are compelling a child to accept an arranged match and holding a child to a betrothal made for her.

rulings.topic: Putting away a wife: the seven grounds and their consequences
rulings.question: On what grounds, if any besides adultery and desertion, may a husband of our house put away his wife, and does her son still honor and mourn her afterward?
rulings.practice: Put away your wife for any of the seven grounds (disobedience to your parents, no son, adultery, jealousy, foul disease, talkativeness, theft), sparing her only in the three cases, and once she is put away let her son no longer mourn her as his mother.

held_by.quote: 出婦之義，必送之。接以賓客之禮 — When putting away a wife, one must escort her and treat her as a guest.
為婦若此，為夫者宜棄之，為有司者治其罪可也。 — For a wife like this, the husband should divorce her, and the magistrate may punish her crime.
The messenger, accompanying her, then discharged his commission.
When the wife went away from her husband, she sent a messenger and took leave of him.

held_by.citation: Liji, Sang Fu Xiao Ji II.25
held_by.quote: A son who was or would be his fathers successor did not wear mourning for his divorced mother. He did not wear such mourning, because one engaged in mourning rites could not offer sacrifice.

held_by.citation: Liji, Sang Fu Xiao Ji I.1 … Sang Fu Xiao Ji I.22
held_by.quote: The son who was his father's successor (as now head of the family) did not wear mourning for his mother who had been divorced.
If the son of the divorced wife have been appointed by the father as his successor, then he does not wear mourning for his mother.
while she was my wife, she was Pâi's mother; but when she ceased to be my wife, she was no longer his mother.

held_by.citation: Liji, Sang Fu Xiao Ji I.1 … Sang Fu Xiao Ji I.22
held_by.quote: the concubine, (following her out of the harem), did not wear mourning for her son.

겨집의 닐곱가지 내팀이 잇ᄂᆞ니 父母ᄭᅴ 順티 아니커든 내티며 아ᄃᆞᆯ 업거든 내티며 淫란커든 내티며 — There are seven grounds for expelling a wife: if she is disobedient to parents, expel her; if she has no son, expel her; if she is adulterous, expel her
不順父母去, 無子去, 淫去, 妬去, 有惡疾去, 多言去, 竊盜去. — disobedient to parents, no son, adultery, jealousy, foul disease, talkativeness, theft.
세 가지 내티디 아니미 잇ᄂᆞ니 取ᄒᆞᆫ 배 잇고 갈배 업거든 내티디 말며 — There are three cases not to expel: if she has a home but no place to go back to, do not expel her
有所取, 無所歸, 不去. 與更三年喪, 不去. 前貧賤後富貴, 不去. — if she has no place to return, do not divorce; if she has mourned three years with you, do not divorce; if you were poor and then rich, do not divorce.
既娶而防之以禮...若妻實犯禮而出之，乃義也。 — After marrying, restrain her by ritual; if she truly violates it, to divorce is righteous.

grounds.citation: Matthew 19:8–9
grounds.quote: Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so. And I say unto you, Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery
grounds.point: Christ withdraws Moses' permission and allows putting away only for fornication.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 24.6
grounds.quote: nothing but adultery, or such wilful desertion as can no way be remedied, by the Church, or Civil Magistrate, is cause sufficient of dissolving the bond of marriage
grounds.point: The Confession admits adultery and irremediable desertion only.

grounds.citation: 1 Corinthians 7:15
grounds.quote: But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases
grounds.point: Desertion frees the deserted spouse.

grounds.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, What the dutie of a wife is toward her husband.
grounds.quote: And therefore no man may put away his wife ... for any cause, except for whoredome, which must be duly prooued before a lawfull Iudge.
grounds.point: The Puritan household manual allows putting away only for proven adultery.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 4 · Of barrennesse, that it hindereth not mariage.
grounds.quote: Impotent persons cannot yeeld due beneuolence: but such as are barren may.
grounds.point: Gouge: barrenness is no impediment that undoes a marriage.

grounds.citation: Exodus 20:12
grounds.quote: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
grounds.point: The command to honor one's mother has no exception for a divorced mother.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 24:1
grounds.quote: When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement
grounds.point: The law of Moses permitted a bill of divorcement.

grounds.citation: Than Kung, Tan Gong I.i.4
grounds.quote: While she was my wife, she was Pâi's mother; but when she ceased to be my wife, she was no longer his mother.
grounds.point: The Liji's Tan Gong denies that a divorced mother remains her son's mother for mourning.

rulings.allowed: Divorce only for adultery, or for willful desertion that cannot be remedied, and then by a public and orderly process (WCF 24.5-6). A son honors and mourns his mother whatever became of his parents' marriage.
rulings.resolution: Of the seven grounds only adultery stands; Christ allows putting away 'for fornication' and the Confession adds only willful desertion that cannot be remedied. Disobedience to parents, bearing no son, jealousy, disease, talkativeness and theft are no grounds: Moses permitted divorce 'because of the hardness of your hearts', and 'from the beginning it was not so'. Gouge adds that barrenness does not undo a marriage, for 'such as are barren' can still render the marriage duty. The rule that a divorced mother is 'no longer his mother' and is not to be mourned is set aside: the command to honor father and mother admits no such exception.

rulings.topic: Marriage as an indissoluble sacrament
rulings.question: Is marriage a sacrament, valid only in the Church and dissolved by nothing but death, so that even an innocent spouse may never divorce and remarry?
rulings.practice: Hold your marriage as a sacrament celebrated in the Church and bound until death, and never divorce or marry again while your spouse lives, even if you were the one wronged.

held_by.quote: The remarriage of persons divorced from a living, lawful spouse contravenes the plan and law of God as taught by Christ.
they "take on themselves the duty to live in complete continence, that is, by abstinence from the acts proper to married couples."
the marriage bond should not be broken and that a husband or wife, if separated, should not be joined to another even for the sake of offspring
the daily increasing facility of divorce is an obstacle to the restoration of marriage to that state of perfection which the divine Redeemer willed it should possess
divorce separates what God has joined together
A marriage that is ratum et consummatum can be dissolved by no human power and by no cause, except death.
By virtue of the sacramentality of their marriage, spouses are bound to one another in the most profoundly indissoluble manner.
refrain from becoming involved in a new union
It is of the greatest consequence to husband and wife that all these things should be known and well understood by them
marriage normally be celebrated within the Mass... The Eucharist is the very source of Christian marriage.
induce them to regularize their situation in the light of Christian principle

held_by.citation: Homily of the State of Matrimony
held_by.quote: that lawe which forbiddeth that a man shoulde caste out his wyfe what faulte soeuer she be combred with, thou shalt haue a very great rewarde

held_by.citation: Gratissimam Sane, II · THE BRIDEGROOM IS WITH YOU · 18 · At Cana in Galilee
held_by.quote: Spouses and families, remember at what price you have been 'bought'!

held_by.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book I, Chapter 15, II
held_by.quote: the law will not allow it to be unloosed for any cause whatsoever, that arises after the union is made

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Throughout the Three Kingdoms of En, The Solemnization of Marriage.
grounds.quote: ALthough Marriage be no sacrament, nor peculiar to the Church of God, but common to mankind, and of Publique interest in every Commonwealth
grounds.point: The Directory denies that marriage is a sacrament or belongs only to the church.

grounds.citation: The Thirty-nine Articles of Religion, Article XXV, English text of 1571
grounds.quote: Those fyue, commonly called Sacramentes, that is to say, Confirmation, Penaunce, Orders, Matrimonie, and extreme Vnction, are not to be compted, for Sacramentes of the gospel
grounds.point: Matrimony is not a sacrament of the gospel.

grounds.citation: Matthew 19:9
grounds.quote: Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery
grounds.point: Christ's own words make an exception for fornication.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 24.5
grounds.quote: In the case of Adultery after marriage, it is lawful for the innocent party to sue our a Divorce: And, after the Divorce, to marry another, as if the offending party were dead.
grounds.point: The innocent party after adultery may divorce and remarry.

grounds.citation: 1 Corinthians 7:15
grounds.quote: A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace.
grounds.point: A deserted believer is not bound.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 24.6
grounds.quote: a publique, and orderly course of Proceeding, is to be observed; And, the persons concerned in it, not left to their own wills and discretion, in their own Case.
grounds.point: Divorce is never left to the couple's own will.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Of the neere coniunction of man and wife together.
grounds.quote: this couenant cannot be released by any, no not by the mutuall consent of man and wife
grounds.point: Gouge: the marriage covenant cannot be released by mutual consent.

grounds.citation: Code of Canon Law, Can. 1141
grounds.quote: A marriage that is ratum et consummatum can be dissolved by no human power and by no cause, except death.
grounds.point: Canon law holds a consummated marriage dissoluble by nothing but death.

rulings.allowed: Marriage is lifelong, God's ordinance, and not to be dissolved by the couple's own will or mutual consent. It is solemnized with the Word and prayer. A marriage made outside the church is still a true marriage.
rulings.resolution: Much of this practice is ours too. Marriage is made by God, the bond 'cannot be released by any, no not by the mutuall consent of man and wife', and divorce is never left to the parties' 'own wills and discretion'. But marriage is 'no sacrament, nor peculiar to the Church of God, but common to mankind', so a civil marriage is a true marriage. And Christ's own exception stands: after adultery the innocent party may divorce and 'marry another, as if the offending party were dead', and desertion frees the deserted. So we set aside the sacramental doctrine, and the rule that no cause but death dissolves a marriage and that the wronged spouse may never remarry.

rulings.topic: A woman's death or mutilation for fidelity: widow suicide and chastity unto death
rulings.question: Must a wife or daughter of our house ever die with her husband, or choose death or mutilation rather than be violated?
rulings.practice: If your husband dies, follow him in death, and rather than let any man touch or take you, kill yourself or let your body be cut.

held_by.quote: 古之節婦，有以死徇其夫者，況敢庸奴其夫乎？ — Of old, chaste wives died for their husbands; how could they treat their husbands as slaves?

held_by.citation: Jia Fan, 6 (女 孫 伯叔父 姪) 5–24
held_by.quote: 吾寧就死，義不受辱 — I would rather die than suffer dishonor.

held_by.citation: Samgang Haengsildo, 烈 35 金氏同窆
held_by.quote: ᄒᆞᆫ ᄃᆞᆯ 나마 밥 아니 먹고 믈ᄲᅮᆫ 먹거늘 — For a month she ate no rice, only drank water.
妾은 王義예 죽고 王 즐김애 죽디 아니ᄒᆞ노이다 — I die for the king's righteousness, not for his pleasure.

도ᄌᆞ기 오ᄂᆞ니 내 어마님 여희여 가아 주구려 ᄒᆞ노ᅌᅵ다 — Bandits are coming; I will leave you and die
ᄒᆞᆫ ᄇᆞᆯ 버히고 ᄯᅩ ᄒᆞᆫ 발 버휴ᄃᆡ ᄉᆞᆫᄌᆡ 듣디 아니커늘 — They cut off one foot, then another, but she did not yield.
나ᄂᆞᆫ 士大夫ㅅ ᄯᆞ리오 僕射ㅅ 겨지비로니 오ᄂᆞᆯ 죽디ᄫᅵ 현마 도ᄌᆞᄀᆡ 겨집 아니 ᄃᆞ외요리라 — I am the daughter of a gentleman and the wife of a high official; today I will die rather than become the wife of a robber.

내 겨지비라셔 節介ㅣ 受티 몯ᄒᆞ고 이 소니 ᄂᆞᄆᆡ게 쥐유니 ᄒᆞᆫ 소ᄂᆞ로 몸 조쳐 더레유미 몯ᄒᆞ리라 — As a woman I have failed in chastity; since my body has been touched by another's hand, I cannot keep it clean with one hand.

grounds.citation: Exodus 20:13–14

grounds.point: We are bound to preserve our own life and may defend it against violence.

grounds.point: A woman who is forced bears no guilt.

grounds.quote: But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm
grounds.point: The apostle stopped a man from killing himself in despair.

grounds.citation: Genesis 39:12
grounds.quote: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.
grounds.point: Joseph kept his chastity by fleeing, not by dying.

grounds.citation: Jia Fan, juan 9 (妻下)
grounds.quote: 古之節婦，有以死徇其夫者
grounds.point: Sima Guang's Jia Fan praises the chaste wives of old who died for their husbands.

rulings.allowed: A wife or daughter may resist, flee, refuse consent and defend her life against violence, and grieve her husband deeply. If she is forced, she is without sin and without shame.
rulings.resolution: God forbids all taking away of one's own life and requires lawful care to preserve it. Scripture says of a woman forced in the field, 'there is in the damsel no sin worthy of death', so violation brings no guilt that death must wash away. The Heidelberg Catechism forbids us to 'hurt my selfe'. So no woman of our house is to follow her husband in death, kill or starve herself rather than be taken, or cut her own body; the Jia Fan's praise of the chaste wives of old who died for their husbands is set aside. What remains is Joseph's way: resist, flee, and leave the garment behind.

rulings.topic: Women ruled by nature: silent, domestic and secluded
rulings.question: Is a woman of our house ruled because she is by nature inferior, and is she to keep silent and stay within the inner quarters?
rulings.practice: Rule your wife because the male is by nature superior; let her keep silence and keep to food, clothing and ceremonies, and let no woman of the house go out of the inner quarters without cause.

held_by.quote: the male is by nature superior, and the female inferior; and the one rules, and the other is ruled; this principle, of necessity, extends to all mankind.
the male is by nature fitter for command than the female
Silence is a woman's glory
令僕子非有警急修葺，不得入中門；婦女婢妾無故不得出中門。 — Order that male servants, except for urgent repairs, may not enter the inner gate; women and maids may not go out without reason.
君子ᄅᆞᆯ 도와 그 不足ᄒᆞᆫ 거ᄉᆞᆯ 勸ᄒᆞᆯ ᄲᅮᆫ이넌뎡 — Should only assist the gentleman and encourage what is lacking.
守家法，不聽婦人言而已
긔걸을 閨門에 내디 아니ᄒᆞ며 일이 음식을 이 밧ᄂᆞᆫ ᄉᆞ이예 이실 ᄯᆞᄅᆞᆷ이니라 — she does not put her steps outside the women's quarters; her work is only in serving food

held_by.citation: Bai Hu Tong, 白虎通 卷9 嫁娶 37

held_by.quote: 겨지븨 法은 ... 바ᄆᆡ 堂애 ᄂᆞ리디 아니ᄒᆞᄂᆞ니 ... 義ᄅᆞᆯ 守ᄒᆞ야 주그니만 몯ᄒᆞ니라 — A wife's law: at night do not go down from the hall without matron; keep righteousness unto death.

grounds.citation: Genesis 1:27
grounds.quote: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
grounds.point: Man and woman alike bear God's image.

grounds.citation: 1 Peter 3:7

grounds.point: Husband and wife are co-heirs of grace, and the wife is owed honor.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 6 · Of husbands high account of wiues.
grounds.quote: Her place is indeed a place of inferiority, and subiection, yet the neerest to equality that may be
grounds.point: Gouge grounds a wife's subjection in her place, not in her nature, and calls it the nearest to equality.

grounds.citation: Titus 2:5
grounds.quote: discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands
grounds.point: Scripture gives the wife a home-keeping calling under her husband.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Of aberrations contrary to a wiues subiection in doing things without or against their husbands consent.
grounds.quote: Such as thinke their houses a prison vnto them, that cannot ... long tarrie at home: they thinke they haue power to goe when and whither they will
grounds.point: Gouge reproves wives who go abroad at their own pleasure against their husbands' minds.

grounds.citation: Proverbs 31:16
grounds.quote: She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard.
grounds.point: The virtuous wife goes out, buys land and works it, so she is not secluded.

grounds.citation: Proverbs 31:26
grounds.quote: She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
grounds.point: The virtuous wife speaks with wisdom; she is not silent.

grounds.citation: Politics, Book I, Chapter 5
grounds.quote: the male is by nature superior, and the female inferior; and the one rules, and the other is ruled
grounds.point: Aristotle grounds a husband's rule in the female's natural inferiority.

rulings.allowed: The husband is head of his wife and she is subject to him as to her place. Her chief calling is her household, kept with discretion and not idly abroad. She may still go out on the family's business, buy and sell, and speak with wisdom, and she is her husband's yoke-fellow and co-heir of grace.
rulings.resolution: Scripture and the Puritans keep a husband's rule and a wife's domestic calling: wives are to be 'keepers at home' and 'obedient to their own husbands', and Gouge reproves wives who treat their houses as 'a prison' and go 'when and whither they will'. But they ground this in the wife's 'place', 'the neerest to equality that may be', not in any natural inferiority. Man and woman alike bear God's image and are 'heirs together of the grace of life'. The virtuous wife of Proverbs 31 buys a field, trades with merchants and 'openeth her mouth with wisdom'. So we set aside Aristotle's claim that the female is 'by nature' inferior, the demand that a wife keep silence, and seclusion within inner quarters.

rulings.topic: Status and lineage in marriage and rank
rulings.question: Do we match marriages and rank people by family background, hereditary status and blood?
rulings.practice: Study the other family's genealogy and take no wife from a rebellious, criminal or diseased house; keep your hereditary station, let rank lessen your mourning for lower kin, and admit no outsider to the lineage's rites.

held_by.quote: 겨집이 다ᄉᆞᆺ 取티 아니홈이잇ᄂᆞ니 반逆ᄒᆞᆫ 집 ᄌᆞ식을 取티 말며 어즈러온 집 ᄌᆞ식을 取티말며 — There are five kinds not to take: do not take a daughter of a rebellious house; do not take a daughter of a disorderly house
逆家子, 不取, 亂家子, 不取, 世有刑人, 不取, 世有惡疾, 不取, 喪父長子, 不取. — rebellious family daughter, disorderly family daughter, family with criminals, family with hereditary disease, fatherless eldest daughter.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 향약의 종류
held_by.quote: 상하간의 수분을 강조하여 신분제 질서를 유지 — “They sought to maintain the status order by emphasizing the duty of each to keep his place between superior and inferior.”

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture, 문중 · 특징 및 의의
held_by.quote: 비혈연자의 참여를 엄격히 통제하여 혈연의 순수성을 특히 강조하며 — Strictly control the participation of non-kin and especially emphasize the purity of blood.

held_by.citation: Sangbyeon Tonggo, 常變通攷 卷九 · 服制 · 服制
held_by.quote: 大夫降其庶子 — a minister reduces mourning for his son by a concubine
혼사를 성립시키기 위해서는 족보에 등재되는 인물들과 그 자녀들의 인신 정보를 훤히 꿰뚫고 있는 보학의 발달이 요구되었다 — To establish a marriage, knowledge of genealogy that thoroughly grasped the personal information of those recorded was required.

grounds.citation: Acts 17:26

grounds.point: All people are of one blood, so no lineage is purer than another.

grounds.citation: James 2:1

grounds.point: Rank is not to govern how Christians treat one another.

grounds.citation: Ezekiel 18:19–20

grounds.citation: Matthew 1:5

grounds.point: Christ's own line received outsiders, Rahab and Ruth.

grounds.citation: Romans 12:16

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 24.3
grounds.quote: Yet, is it the duty of Christians to marry only in the Lord
grounds.point: The test that matters in a match is faith.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Of equalitie in estat• and condition betwixt those that are to be maried together.
grounds.quote: that Princes, Nobles, and Gentlemen, mary such as are of their owne ranke: and the meaner sort such as are of their degree.
grounds.point: Gouge counsels marrying within one's own rank.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 54 · Direction to parents in prouiding mariages.
grounds.quote: the match prouided must not be too neere of kin, of a contrary religion, of too vnequall an age, of too great disparity in estate.
grounds.point: Gouge counts too great a disparity of estate against a match.

rulings.allowed: Inquire into a prospective spouse's faith, life and family, marry only in the Lord, and seek a fitting match in age, estate and condition, as Gouge counsels.
rulings.resolution: Some care for station in marriage is Puritan counsel and we keep it: Gouge advises 'some equalitie' of estate and condition and warns against 'too great disparity in estate', and the Confession forbids marrying the 'notoriously wicked'. But God 'hath made of one blood all nations of men', faith is not to be held 'with respect of persons', and 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father'. So we set aside refusing a woman because her house had a rebel, a criminal or a disease, or because she is a fatherless eldest daughter. We set aside guarding the 'purity' of the blood: Rahab and Ruth stand in Christ's own line. And we set aside lessening one's mourning for kin of lower rank.

rulings.topic: Marriage rules beyond the moral law: canon impediments and the levirate
rulings.question: Do we keep the church's added marriage impediments and the Levitical levirate duty beyond the moral law of Leviticus 18?
rulings.practice: Do not marry within the canonical degrees of affinity, a godparent's kin or your deceased wife's sister, and if your brother dies childless, marry his widow to raise up offspring for him.

held_by.quote: The impediment of public propriety arises from an invalid marriage after the establishment of common life or from notorious or public concubinage.

it commanded the next kinsman that was liuing and free to marie her, that he might raise vp seed to his brother deceased
the widow reiected was to loose his shooe from his foot, and to spit in his face in the presence of the Elders

grounds.point: The Confession treats affinity as near as blood, which bars a deceased wife's sister.

grounds.point: Massachusetts forbade marriage to a deceased wife's sister.
