grounds.citation: The Second Helvetic Confession, chapters IV, V, XXVI and XXIX, Second Helvetic Confession 26
grounds.quote: we should make honorable mention of those who died in the Lord, and perform all duties of love to those they leave behind, as their widows and fatherless children. Other care for the dead we do not enjoin.
grounds.point: The Reformed churches name the duties owed after death: honorable mention and love to the survivors, and no other care for the dead.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 47 · Of childrens paying their parents debts after their death.
grounds.quote: Three things there be which children must make conscience of, euen in regard of their deceased parents credit, and reputation; one, to pay their debts: another, to suppresse ill rumors: a third, to imitate their good example.
grounds.point: Gouge sets out what children still owe dead parents: paying their debts, guarding their name, and following their example.

grounds.citation: W. A. P. Martin, "The Worship of Ancestors: a Plea for Toleration," Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 627
grounds.quote: The idea of offering food to the dead is not in accordance with our habits of thought, but it cannot be denied that such offering may be made the vehicle of an innocent and beautiful sentiment.
grounds.point: The dissent: Martin held that food offered to the dead can express an innocent sentiment.

rulings.allowed: Honor and support parents while they live. After their death, speak of them with honor, care for the widow and the fatherless they leave, pay their debts, defend their good name, and follow their good example.
rulings.resolution: The seasonal sacrifices to departed parents and forebears are set aside. Food given for the dead is exactly what the faithful Israelite swore he had not given (Deuteronomy 26:14), eating the sacrifices of the dead is named among Israel's sins (Psalm 106:28), and sacrifice is religious worship owed to God alone (WCF 21.2), which Calvin says the heathen stole from God when they sacrificed to departed heroes. Martin's plea that the offering can carry an innocent sentiment does not answer Deuteronomy, which forbids the gift itself and not only a bad motive, and the dead know nothing of it (Ecclesiastes 9:5). Serving the dead as the living is fulfilled instead by the duties the Reformed name: honorable mention, care for those they left, paying their debts, guarding their name and following their example.

grounds.quote: But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 21.2
grounds.quote: Religious Worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; and to him alone; not, to Angels, Saints, or any other Creature
grounds.point: The libations and prayer of the death-day rite are religious worship, which is given to God alone.

grounds.citation: H. Blodget, "The Attitude of Christianity toward Ancestral Worship," Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 651
grounds.quote: Even though the avowed aim be declared to be purely subjective, and without any reference to good or evil imparted to, or received from, the dead, yet that which is done, as prostrations, libations, offerings, prayers, one or all of them imply, in their natural and obvious meaning, communication with some external object.
grounds.point: Even a death-day rite said to be purely an expression of feeling still, by its libations, offerings and prayers, addresses the dead.

grounds.citation: A Fruitfull and Usefull Discourse touching the Honour due from Children to Paren, CHAP. II. Of Honour in generall due to Parents.
grounds.quote: When they do not so soon forget their Parents after they are dead and gone.
grounds.point: Not forgetting dead parents is part of the honor children owe them.

grounds.citation: Report of the Committee on Ancestral Worship (J. Jackson, chairman), Records of the China Centenary Missionary Conference (Shanghai, 1907), p. 240
grounds.quote: the death days of our members should be observed with special memorial celebrations of the Holy Communion or other appropriate services, both in the churches and at the graves
grounds.point: The Protestant remedy was not to forget the death-day but to keep it as a day of Christian remembrance.

rulings.allowed: Keep the anniversary of a parent's or forebear's death as a day of remembrance: gather the family, speak of the person's life and example, give thanks to God for them in family or church worship, and visit the grave.
rulings.resolution: The death-day offering is set aside; the remembrance of the day is kept. Bringing out the tablet and presenting wine, food and a prayer to the dead treats as present one who shall not return (2 Samuel 12:23) and knows not any thing (Ecclesiastes 9:5), and it gives what Deuteronomy forbids to give for the dead. Blodget answers the plea that the rite is only inward feeling: libations, offerings and prayers by their natural meaning imply communication with the dead. What is kept is not forgetting parents once they are dead and gone (Cobbett), with the day observed, as the 1907 committee urged, by Christian remembrance.

rulings.allowed: Keep Seollal, Chuseok, harvest and the other festival days as family gatherings with their customary foods; give the first of the increase to the Lord and thanks to God for each new harvest; say grace before meals.
rulings.resolution: Offering festival foods and each new grain and fruit to the ancestors before eating is set aside. The first of the increase is owed to the LORD (Proverbs 3:9; Exodus 23:19), and in the very law of the tithe the faithful declared that none of it had been given for the dead (Deuteronomy 26:14). Food is received from God with thanksgiving and eaten to his glory (1 Timothy 4:4; 1 Corinthians 10:31), and thanksgivings at their seasons are part of his worship (WCF 21.5), so the first portion and the thanks go to him. The festival days themselves, their foods and the gathering of kin are harmless customs and remain.

grounds.quote: all prostrations, libations, offerings, prayers, thanksgivings to the dead, whether before the coffin, or in the ancestral hall at the various times for such worship each year, or at the tombs on the occasion of the annual festival called the Ch‘ing-ming.
grounds.point: The prostrations, libations, offerings and prayers at the tombs are named among the practices the Christian faith opposes.

grounds.quote: care for the place in which those who have gone before sleep their last sleep, with tasteful adornments of the same, the erection there of headstones and monuments in Christian taste, and with Christian inscriptions, and such loving visits to the spot as the necessities of life and a healthful regard for duties to the living may permit

grounds.citation: Resolution IV as adopted, Records of the China Centenary Missionary Conference (Shanghai, 1907), p. 624
grounds.quote: encourage an affectionate remembrance of the dead by beautifying graves and erecting useful memorials to parents and ancestors
grounds.point: The 1907 Conference urged beautifying graves and raising memorials as the Christian form of remembrance.

grounds.citation: W. A. P. Martin, "The Worship of Ancestors: a Plea for Toleration," Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 627
grounds.quote: In our native land no one finds fault with the presentation of floral offerings at funerals, or at the graves of the departed, and if it is legitimate to deck a grave with flowers, why is it not so to offer fruits or meats?
grounds.point: The dissent: Martin argued that if flowers at a grave are lawful, food offerings must be too.

rulings.allowed: Visit the family graves on Hansik, Chuseok, Memorial Day or any fitting day; sweep, weed, repair and plant them; set up headstones and memorials with Christian inscriptions; lay flowers; and spend the time in remembrance and in fitting talk among the living. No food, wine, prayer or bow is offered to the dead at the tomb.
rulings.resolution: Going to the graves, sweeping and adorning them, and remembering the dead there are kept; the food, libations, prayer and bows offered to the ancestors at the tomb are set aside. The grave is a memorial (Genesis 35:20) and a place to be cared for and lovingly visited (Blodget; 1907 Resolution IV), but food set out for the dead is what Deuteronomy 26:14 forbids, no rite at the grave profits the dead (the Westminster Directory), and Blodget names the prostrations, libations, offerings and prayers at the tombs among what the faith sets itself against. Martin asked why, if flowers are lawful, fruits and meats are not: flowers adorn the place for the living, while food and wine are set out to be eaten and drunk by the one they are given to, which is giving for the dead. The old saints honored their dead enough when they buried them honestly (Second Helvetic).

grounds.quote: that which is done, as prostrations, libations, offerings, prayers, one or all of them imply, in their natural and obvious meaning, communication with some external object.
grounds.point: The officiant's libations and prayers are not mere ceremony; by their plain meaning they address the dead.

grounds.citation: Joshua 24:15
grounds.quote: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
grounds.point: The head's office in his household's worship is kept, but it is exercised toward the LORD.

rulings.allowed: The head leads the household's worship of God, and members take their parts in it: reading Scripture, praying, singing psalms, and preparing the family's gatherings and meals with care and order.
rulings.resolution: No member of the family takes an officiant's part in an ancestral offering: the fasting and purification for it, the incense, the three libations, the prayer-reading and the setting out of dishes are set aside. Scripture describes just such a household division of labor, children, fathers and women each with a part, in making offerings to other gods (Jeremiah 7:18), and it forbids worship God did not command or copied from the nations (Leviticus 10:1; Deuteronomy 12:30; WCF 21.1; WLC 109, which expressly refuses the plea of antiquity and custom). The libations and prayers are not neutral ceremony, since by their natural meaning they address the dead (Blodget). The head's office over the household's worship is kept, directed to the LORD (Joshua 24:15).

(When the representative of the departed) had made the libation with the kiâ cup, or the horn, (the sacrificer) was told (to bow to him) and put him at ease.

grounds.point: Living men may not receive sacrifice and worship; the apostles treated the attempt as an outrage.

grounds.quote: Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and worshipped him. But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 18:11

grounds.point: The law forbids every go-between who makes the dead present to the living.

grounds.point: The living are not to seek the dead, whether through a medium or a stand-in.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 21.2

grounds.point: The offerings and bows made to the personator are religious worship, which is given to God alone.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 47 · Of childrens paying their parents debts after their death.
grounds.quote: Parents themselues cannot doe any thing when they are dead to preserue the same: children therefore being the liuing Image of their parents must indeuour to doe it.
grounds.point: Children are their parents' living image by preserving their name and example, not by impersonating them in a rite.

rulings.allowed: Descendants show themselves the living image of their forebears by guarding their good name and following their good example.
rulings.resolution: No descendant sits as the personator of the dead, and no one bows to him or serves him as the ancestor's spirit. The personator is set up so that the dead may be present among the living to receive offerings and bows; the apostles tore their clothes when men tried to offer sacrifice to them (Acts 14:14-15), and Peter refused even a prostration that Calvin judges was offered without intent to adore him (Acts 10:25-26). To make a living man the stand-in through whom the dead receive offerings is to seek the dead through the living, which the law forbids (Deuteronomy 18:11; Isaiah 8:19). A grandson rightly represents his grandfather by being his living image in character and in guarding his name (Gouge).

grounds.citation: 1 Corinthians 10:21
grounds.quote: Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils.
grounds.point: Christ's people may not share the meal of a sacrifice offered to others.

grounds.citation: Psalms 106:28

grounds.point: Food openly received as a sacrificial portion is to be declined.

grounds.citation: Report of the Committee on Ancestral Worship (J. Jackson, chairman), Records of the China Centenary Missionary Conference (Shanghai, 1907), pp. 226-227
grounds.quote: The sacrificial offerings at the worship of ancestors are simply the materials of a feast, at which the … living and the dead are supposed to meet together.
grounds.point: The sacrificial meal is understood as a communion feast of the living with the dead, so taking the blessing portion is taking part in it.

grounds.citation: James 1:17
grounds.quote: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights
grounds.point: Blessing and food come from God, not from the ancestors, so they are not received as the ancestors' gift.

grounds.citation: Nehemiah 8:10
grounds.quote: Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared
grounds.point: A feast on a holy day, with portions sent to those who have nothing, is commended.

grounds.citation: 1 Corinthians 10:25–27
grounds.quote: Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake … If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go; whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake.
grounds.point: The dissent from Scripture itself: food as such is not defiled, and a Christian may eat at an unbeliever's table without asking.

rulings.allowed: Hold family feasts at the festivals and gatherings, assemble all the kin, send portions to those who have nothing and share with the household's helpers, and give thanks to God for the food. At an unbelieving relative's table, eat what is set before you without asking; if food is named as offered to the dead, decline it courteously for conscience' sake.
rulings.resolution: Receiving the blessing portion and eating the sacrificial food as the ancestors' gift is set aside; the family meal itself, with the kin gathered and portions sent to those who have nothing, is kept. The meal of the rite is the feast at which the living and the dead are supposed to meet (the 1907 report, after Legge), and eating it as the dead's blessing is eating the sacrifices of the dead (Psalm 106:28) at a table Christ's people cannot share (1 Corinthians 10:21). Paul's liberty to eat what is sold or set before us without asking (1 Corinthians 10:25, 27) is the dissent, and Paul himself answers it: once food is named as offered, we decline it for conscience' sake (10:28). Every good gift comes from the Father of lights (James 1:17), so the thanks for the meal go to him.

grounds.citation: 2 Samuel 12:22–23
grounds.quote: While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept: for I said, Who can tell whether GOD will be gracious to me, that the child may live? But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.

rulings.allowed: Mourn with the moderate grief the apostle allows, bury the dead decently, and care for the widow and children they leave behind; the anniversaries may be kept as days of remembrance under the death-day ruling.
rulings.resolution: The sacrifices of the mourning cycle, repose, end of wailing, attaching the tablet, and the first- and second-year sacrifices, are set aside. They exist to settle the dead parent's spirit and install it among the ancestors, but at death the soul returns at once to God, to heaven or to hell, and Scripture knows no third place (WCF 32.1; Hebrews 9:27; the Homily); the believer departs to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23) and needs no duty of the living (Second Helvetic). The 1907 report adds that once a man knows that living or dying we are the Lord's, sacrifice with such a motive is impossible. David's rule stands: he fasted while the child lived and, once it died, rose and submitted (2 Samuel 12:22-23); moderate mourning is lawful, but sacrifices to bring the dead to rest are not.

grounds.quote: Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and worshipped him. But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Concerning Buriall of the Dead.
grounds.quote: the customes of kneeling down, and praying by, or towards the dead Corps, and other such usages, in the place where it lies, before it be carried to Buriall, are Superstitious … That this shall not extend to deny any civill respects or differences at the Buriall, suitable to the ranke and condition of the party deceased whiles he was living.

grounds.citation: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, Chapters 11-12, Section I.12.3
grounds.quote: True, we often read that men were worshipped; but that was, if I may so speak, civil honour. The case is different with religious honour, which, the moment it is conjoined with worship, carries profanation of the divine honour along with it.
grounds.point: The same outward act is civil honor between people and religious honor once it is joined to worship.

grounds.citation: W. A. P. Martin, "The Worship of Ancestors: a Plea for Toleration," Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 626
grounds.quote: The posture is always that of kneeling, alternated with prostrations—in the worship of the most exalted divinity there is no other—but it does not in itself form an act of idolatry, because the same posture is employed to show respect to the living. … I have seen a Russian widow kneel in the street and bow her head in the dust before the coffin that contained the remains of her husband. In that act there was nothing idolatrous, or even religious—the deceased not being a calendar saint.
grounds.point: The dissent: Martin, whose conclusion the 1890 Conference rejected, held that kneeling before the dead is no more than the respect shown the living.

grounds.citation: Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, Plane compertum est (8 Dec. 1939), AAS 32 (1940), pp. 24-26, Prooemium and art. 4
grounds.quote: nonnullas caeremonias, licet antiquitus cum ethnicis ritibus connexae essent, in praesentiarum, mutatis saeculorum fluxu moribus et animis, civilem tantum servare significationem pietatis in antenatos … Inclinationes capitis atque aliae civilis observantiae manifestationes ante defunctos vel defunctorum imagines, et etiam ante tabellam defuncti, simplici nomine inscriptam, uti licitae et honestae habendae sunt.
grounds.point: The Catholic dissent: because changed custom has left certain ceremonies once tied to heathen rites only a civil meaning of piety toward ancestors, inclinations of the head before the dead, their images, and a tablet bearing the simple name are to be held lawful.

rulings.allowed: Bow to living parents, grandparents and elders, including the chief mourners at a funeral; at a funeral and burial show the civil respects suited to the dead person's rank and condition in life. No bow, kneeling or prostration is directed to the dead, the coffin, a tablet, a portrait or a grave.
rulings.resolution: Bowing and prostration before the dead, the coffin, the tablets and the shrine are set aside; bowing to the living is untouched, and we grant the dissent its premise that the posture in itself is no idolatry, since the same bow is rightly given to the living (Genesis 23:7; Martin). The line is drawn by the person the bow is given to and the act it belongs to: civil honor passes between the living, but a bow joined to a religious rite becomes religious honor (Calvin), and the bows of this rite greet the spirits as they are received at the tablet and take leave of them as they are sent off, which is a greeting to forebears who do not know us (Isaiah 63:16) and religious honor to creatures (WLC 105). Peter refused a prostration Cornelius surely did not mean as idolatry (Acts 10:25-26), and the Westminster Directory calls kneeling towards the dead body superstitious while keeping every civil respect at the burial, which answers Martin's widow kneeling before her husband's coffin. Plane compertum allows only inclinations of the head, before a tablet with the bare name, on the ground that changed custom has left the ceremonies a merely civil meaning; that ground fails where the bow still greets and dismisses the spirits, and for this family the Westminster standards outweigh it.

prayers which express the filial piety... all being done to please the souls of the departed

grounds.citation: Ecclesiastes 9:5–6

grounds.point: The dead do not know what is offered and have no share in the meal set out for them.

grounds.citation: Luke 16:26
grounds.quote: between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us
grounds.point: The dead do not cross over to be present at the living's table.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 26:14
grounds.quote: I have not eaten thereof in my mourning, neither have I taken away ought thereof for any unclean use, nor given ought thereof for the dead
grounds.point: Whatever the belief behind it, food given for the dead is forbidden.

grounds.citation: Psalms 115:14–17
grounds.quote: The LORD shall increase you more and more, you and your children. Ye are blessed of the LORD which made heaven and earth. The heaven, even the heavens, are the LORD's: but the earth hath he given to the children of men. The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence.
grounds.point: Increase and blessing on our children come from the LORD; the dead are silent, so the blessing is not sought from them.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 32.1
grounds.quote: the Souls of the Righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest Heavens, where they behold the face of God … Beside these two Places, for Souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none.
grounds.point: The souls of the dead are in heaven or hell, not at the shrine waiting to eat.

grounds.citation: The Second Helvetic Confession, chapters IV, V, XXVI and XXIX, Second Helvetic Confession 26
grounds.quote: that which is recorded of the spirits or souls of the dead sometimes appearing to them that are alive, and craving certain duties of them whereby they may be set free: we count those apparitions among the delusions, crafts, and deceits of the Devil
grounds.point: Spirits of the dead that appear and ask the living for food or service are not to be credited or served.

grounds.citation: H. Blodget, "The Attitude of Christianity toward Ancestral Worship," Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 651
grounds.quote: If really present, the ancestors should, on every account, be sacrificed to as though present. If their presence were uncertain, or if they were not really present, still it would be necessary to regard them as present … Even though the avowed aim be declared to be purely subjective, and without any reference to good or evil imparted to, or received from, the dead, yet that which is done, as prostrations, libations, offerings, prayers, one or all of them imply, in their natural and obvious meaning, communication with some external object. Without this they are like a dumb show, or senseless pantomime
grounds.point: The rule of sacrificing as if the dead were present fails both ways: if they are thought present it is communion with the dead, and if not it is an empty show.

grounds.citation: W. A. P. Martin, "The Worship of Ancestors: a Plea for Toleration," Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 627
grounds.quote: it is the object of worship, not the offering that constitutes idolatry. … It means that the spirit still remembers its kindred and joins them in their commemorative feast.
grounds.point: The dissent: Martin defended food offerings as meaning that the spirit remembers its kin and joins their feast.

rulings.allowed: Remember the dead and speak of them with love; ask God, not the dead, for blessing on the family and its children.
rulings.resolution: Offering to the dead as present, waiting while the spirits eat, and seeking their blessing are set aside, and this is the root of the other rulings on ancestral rites. The dead know not any thing and have no portion in anything done under the sun (Ecclesiastes 9:5-6), a great gulf is fixed between them and us (Luke 16:26), their souls are with God in heaven or shut up in hell with no third place from which they come to a meal (WCF 32.1), and spirits of the dead that appear asking for food are deceits of the devil (Second Helvetic). Blessing on our children comes from the LORD who made heaven and earth, while the dead praise him not (Psalm 115:14-17), so it is sought from him alone. Martin's dissent, that the offering means the spirit remembers its kin and joins their feast, states the very belief Scripture denies; the softer form, sacrificing as if they were present while professing not to know, Blodget answers, since the offerings either mean communication with the dead or are a dumb show, and either way Deuteronomy 26:14 forbids the gift.

rulings.topic: Four-generation rule, removal of tablets, and unremoved ancestors
rulings.question: Will we keep spirit tablets of our forebears, sacrifice before them up to the great-great-grandfather, bury each tablet as its generation passes, and keep the tablets of honored founders unremoved forever? And how far back must a house carry its remembrance?
rulings.practice: Sacrifice to your forebears up to the great-great-grandfather, bury each tablet as its generation passes, and keep the tablet of a meritorious founder unremoved for all generations.

grounds.point: The tablet of this rite is not a mere memorial but the supposed seat of the spirit and a means of intercourse with the dead.

grounds.citation: H. Blodget, "The Attitude of Christianity toward Ancestral Worship", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 639
grounds.quote: the Christian faith will, among its adherents, uniformly and persistently set itself against all superstitious and sinful practices in their treatment of the dead, such as the preparation and use of the ancestral tablet

grounds.citation: Plane compertum est: Instructio circa quasdam caeremonias et iuramentum super ri, 4

grounds.point: Rome (1939) holds bows and other civil signs before the dead and before a tablet inscribed with the bare name lawful; this covers only a name-board, not a consecrated spirit seat with offerings.

grounds.citation: H. Blodget, "The Attitude of Christianity toward Ancestral Worship", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 638
grounds.quote: or the carefully kept family record, whether within or without the folds of the sacred volume; but it will promote and encourage all these things.
grounds.point: What replaces the tablets is the carefully kept family record, which Christianity encourages.

grounds.quote: After this lived Job an hundred and forty years, and saw his sons, and his sons’ sons, [even] four generations.
grounds.point: Four generations is the span a man can know in his own life.

grounds.citation: Psalms 103:15–16
grounds.quote: For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more.
grounds.point: Man is grass; the memory of him passes, and Scripture does not lay on the living a remembrance without end.

grounds.citation: Ecclesiastes 1:11
grounds.quote: [There is] no remembrance of former [things;] neither shall there be [any] remembrance of [things] that are to come with [those] that shall come after.
grounds.point: Remembrance fades by God's ordering of things; a duty to hold it forever asks more than men are given.

grounds.citation: Liji, Da Zhuan 7 (Legge)
grounds.quote: For parties four generations removed (from the same common ancestor) the mourning was reduced to that worn for three months, and this was the limit of wearing the hempen cloth.
grounds.point: The Rites themselves thin the duty generation by generation.

grounds.citation: Liji, Da Zhuan 7 (Legge)
grounds.quote: After the sixth generation the bond of kinship was held to be at an end.
grounds.point: And they set an end to it.

grounds.citation: Mencius 4B.22 (Legge)

grounds.point: Even a sage's influence runs out by the fifth generation.

grounds.citation: Zhu Xi, Family Rituals 1.5 (置祭田)
grounds.quote: 親盡則以為墓田
grounds.point: When kinship is exhausted the house is released and the land becomes grave land: the grave remains when the near duty ends.

grounds.citation: Liji, Da Zhuan 2
grounds.quote: 宗其繼别子之所自出者，百世不遷者也。宗其繼高祖者，五世則遷者也。
grounds.point: Each branch house lets its forebears go at the fifth generation; only the great line keeps its founder for a hundred generations.

rulings.allowed: Each house keeps the near remembrance of its own forebears four generations back, to the great-great-grandparents: their names, their stories, their graves and the day of their death. Beyond the fourth generation the house is released; the older forebears pass into the clan's register, kept by the heir as far as it has come down to him, and the founder is remembered by the whole clan at its gathering. No board or record is treated as the seat of a spirit, and nothing is set out, burned or prayed before it.
rulings.resolution: The tablet and the sacrifice are set aside: the tablet of this rite is made to be the spirit's seat, and the rite sets food and wine before it; that is giving 'ought thereof for the dead' (Deut 26:14) and seeking to the dead on behalf of the living (Isa 8:19), while religious worship belongs to God alone (WCF 21.2). The four-generation span is kept, as a measure of what a house can carry. Job saw four generations, the span a man can know; man is grass, and the place thereof shall know it no more; the Rites thin the duty at each generation and end it after the sixth, and Mencius has even a sage's influence run out at the fifth. So a house is not laid under a remembrance without limit: it carries its own forebears to the great-great-grandparents and is then released, as Zhu Xi turns the land to grave land when kinship is exhausted. Only the great line keeps its founder for a hundred generations, and that is the clan's charge, not every house's.

rulings.topic: Marriage before the ancestors and the bride's presentation (廟見)
rulings.question: Will a bride be presented to her husband's ancestors at a shrine, make offerings before them, and be received into the line by that rite?
rulings.practice: After the wedding, present the bride at the ancestral shrine so that she offers to her husband's ancestors and is received into the line.

grounds.citation: Genesis 2:24
grounds.quote: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
grounds.point: Marriage is made by the union of husband and wife, not by the bride's reception before the ancestors.

grounds.citation: Ruth 4:11
grounds.quote: And all the people that were in the gate, and the elders, said, We are witnesses.
grounds.point: A marriage taking a wife into a line is witnessed before the living kin and elders; this is the core that is kept.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 26:14
grounds.quote: nor given ought thereof for the dead
grounds.point: The bride's offering of vegetables to her dead father-in-law gives part of an offering to the dead, which Scripture forbids.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 21.2
grounds.quote: Religious Worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; and to him alone; not, to Angels, Saints, or any other Creature
grounds.point: Religious worship is for God alone, so a bride may not be brought to worship her husband's ancestors.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Throughout the Three Kingdoms of En, The Solemnization of Marriage.
grounds.quote: Before the solemnizing of Marriage between any Persons, their purpose of Marriage shall be published by the Minister three severall Sabbath dayes in the Congregation
grounds.point: The Reformed way announces a marriage to the living congregation and kin beforehand.

grounds.citation: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, Chapters 11-12, Section I.12.3
grounds.quote: True, we often read that men were worshipped; but that was, if I may so speak, civil honour. The case is different with religious honour, which, the moment it is conjoined with worship, carries profanation of the divine honour along with it.
grounds.point: Bows and honor to living parents-in-law are civil honor; offerings before the dead are religious honor and profane God's honor.

grounds.citation: H. G. Underwood, The Religions of Eastern Asia (1910), Lecture IV, pp. 161-165
grounds.quote: all important events are solemnly announced to the ancestors, marriages are performed in their presence
grounds.point: Underwood, the Presbyterian missionary to Korea, counts performing marriages in the ancestors' presence among the acts that show belief in the dead as spirits.

rulings.allowed: The bride is received into her husband's family before the living: the marriage is made known beforehand, solemnized publicly with the consent of the parents, and witnessed by the kin. She may bow to her living parents-in-law and elders as civil honor, and her name is entered in the family register as a member of the line.
rulings.resolution: Receiving a bride into the family and line is kept, and it is done before the living, as Boaz's marriage was witnessed by 'all the people that were in the gate, and the elders' and as the Directory requires the purpose of marriage to be published and the parents' consent sought. The presentation at the shrine with offerings to the dead parents-in-law is set aside: it gives 'ought thereof for the dead' (Deut 26:14) and gives religious worship to creatures (WCF 21.2), and a marriage is made by leaving father and mother and cleaving to a wife (Gen 2:24), not by the ancestors' acceptance. Calvin's line holds here: bows to living parents are civil honor; offerings to the dead are religious honor.

이들은 자신이 관리하는 토지에서 나온 수확 중 일부로 묘사의 제물을 장만하며, 약간의 소작료를 문중에 낸다. — From the harvest of the land they manage, they prepare the offerings for the grave rites and pay a small rent to the clan.
여기에서 나오는 수입으로 봉제사를 하며 — With the income from this they perform the ancestral rites.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 문중 門中 · 문중 · 내용
held_by.quote: 유명한 조상의 자손들은 문중재산을 적립, 행사를 성대하게 치름으로써 조상의 사회적 지위를 계승하려고 한다 — Descendants accumulate property and hold grand rites to inherit the ancestor's social standing.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 당내친 堂內親 · 당내친 · 내용
held_by.quote: 제사를 주재하는 종손이 비록 소유자는 아니어도 관리는 하였다. — The heir who presides over the rites managed them, though he was not the owner.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 26:14

grounds.citation: Genesis 23:20

grounds.point: Holding family land as a lasting burying place is approved in Scripture; this part is kept.

grounds.citation: 1 Timothy 5:8
grounds.quote: But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
grounds.point: Family wealth is owed to the living kin, which a common fund may serve.

grounds.citation: Resolutions as adopted, IV, Records of the China Centenary Missionary Conference (Shanghai, 1907), p. 624
grounds.quote: by building or endowing churches, schools, hospitals, asylums, and other charitable institutions as is common in all Christian lands, thus making memorials of the departed a means of helping the living through successive generations.
grounds.point: The conference redirects endowments made in the name of the dead to the good of the living.

grounds.citation: J. Jackson, Report of the Committee on Ancestral Worship, Records of the China Centenary Missionary Conference (Shanghai, 1907), p. 243
grounds.quote: This idea might be made use of and the stream of benevolence turned into pious Christian channels by urging rich families to establish memorial schools, hospitals, reformatories and other benevolent institutions.
grounds.point: The wealth families give for ancestral rites should be turned to schools and charity instead.

grounds.citation: W. A. P. Martin, "The Worship of Ancestors: a Plea for Toleration", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), pp. 623-624
grounds.quote: From time to time we hear of the endowment of clan schools, clan cemeteries and clan refuges for the aged poor
grounds.point: Clan endowments have long served schools, cemeteries, and the aged poor; these uses are kept.

grounds.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (한국민족문화대백과사전), 문중 · 내용
grounds.quote: 또한, 문중은 문중산을 소유하여 자손들에게 묘지를 제공하여 준다.
grounds.point: Korean clan property also provides grave sites to descendants, a use that is kept.

rulings.allowed: The family may hold land or a common fund that is not to be sold off lightly, used for the family burying ground and its upkeep, headstones, the family register, gatherings of the clan, education of its children, and relief of poor, aged, widowed, and orphaned kin. Nothing is bought, kept, or spent for offerings to the dead, and no vessels are kept for sacrifice.
rulings.resolution: Common family land and funds are kept, turned to the uses Scripture and the missionaries commend: a burying place held as a possession, as Abraham held Machpelah, and provision for one's own house (1 Tim 5:8), schools, and charity, 'making memorials of the departed a means of helping the living' (1907, Resolution IV). What is set aside is the dedication of land, income, and vessels to the sacrifices: Israel's hallowed tithe was not to be given 'for the dead' (Deut 26:14). Korean clan property already includes the burial mountain, gravestones, and the gathering hall, so the keepable part is large; only the offering purpose is removed.

rulings.topic: The heir's office of carrying on the rites (奉祀) and its succession
rulings.question: Will we name an heir of the eldest line whose office is to preside over the ancestral sacrifices, with rules for who takes it up so the rites never cease?
rulings.practice: As eldest legitimate son, inherit and preside over the ancestral sacrifices; if the line fails, let the next son, a concubine's son, or a daughter's son take them up, and never let the rites cease.

held_by.quote: 往迎爾相，承我宗事，率以敬先妣之嗣 — Go to meet your mate, carry on my ancestral service, and with reverence continue the late mother's line.
He will sacrifice, with the victims belonging to his higher rank, in the house of the eldest son.

the principal in this vicarious service will not conduct the sacrifice so as to see that the spirit of the deceased is satisfied to the full; nor send the cup round among all who are present, nor receive the blessing (at the close); nor lay on the ground the portions of the sacrifice as thank-offerings; nor have with him (the wife of the elder brother)
the eldest son by the wife took the precedence.
prepare two victims, and present the better of them to his chief. He and his wife should together... reverently assist at his sacrifice in the ancestral temple.

did not sacrifice to his grandfather--to show there was the Honoured Head (who should do so)

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 족보 1. 동아시아의 관찬 족보
held_by.quote: 가족 가운데 한 명이 가산과 제사를 단독으로 계승하는 ‘가독상속(家督相續)’을 실시하고 있었다. — One member of the family alone succeeded to the family property and the ancestral rites, practicing 'family head succession'.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 섭사 攝祀
held_by.quote: 적장자가 어려서 제사를 주재할 수 없을 때 그의 삼촌 등이 섭사하였다 — When the eldest legitimate son was too young to preside, his uncle acted as substitute.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 섭사 攝祀
held_by.quote: 적장자가 질병 등인 경우는 그의 아우 등이 대행하였다 — When the eldest legitimate son was ill, his younger brother acted for him.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 21:17
grounds.quote: for he is the beginning of his strength; the right of the firstborn is his.
grounds.point: Scripture recognizes a standing right of the firstborn in the family's inheritance.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 26:14
grounds.quote: nor given ought thereof for the dead
grounds.point: The heir's sacrificial office consists of giving offerings to the dead, which Scripture forbids.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 21.1
grounds.quote: he may not be Worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture.
grounds.point: An office of family sacrifice to ancestors has no warrant in Scripture and so may not be kept as worship.

grounds.citation: Of Domesticall Duties: Eight Treatises, Section 47 · Of childrens paying their parents debts after their death.
grounds.quote: so also to their credit and name, which is a thing of greater account, and honour: a thing wherein they may bring a kinde of blessing to their parents and make them liue after their death.
grounds.point: Gouge charges children with preserving their dead parents' credit and name, a duty about the dead that serves no rite to them.

grounds.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32, III.
grounds.quote: where there are two or more males in equal degree, the eldest only shall inherit
grounds.point: English custom gave the eldest male the inheritance, supporting an office of the eldest line.

grounds.citation: H. G. Underwood, The Religions of Eastern Asia (1910), Lecture IV, pp. 161-165
grounds.quote: coupled with the idea of the necessity that every spirit shall have those who will do him honor and attend to his needs, and that such services can be rendered only by male offspring, has created such an inordinate desire for sons that the absence of them is a warrant for divorce or for taking a concubine.
grounds.point: The rule that a male heir must keep the rites going produced divorce and concubinage, which is why that urgency is set aside.

grounds.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (한국민족문화대백과사전), 보종 · 내용
grounds.quote: 특히 종손은 봉제사(奉祭祀) 외에도 접빈객(接賓客) · 족보편찬 등의 종중의 대내외적인 일로
grounds.point: The Korean heir's office already includes receiving guests and compiling the genealogy besides the rites; those duties are kept.

rulings.allowed: The lineage heir (종손) of the eldest line is kept as an office: he represents the line, keeps the family register and records, sees to the family graves and their markers, hosts and convenes the clan's gatherings, receives kin and guests, and looks after kin in need. Who succeeds to the office follows the family's own rule of succession, decided by the family head. He presides over no sacrifice, and no one is pressed to produce or procure a son so that rites will not cease.
rulings.resolution: The office of the eldest line is kept: Scripture recognizes 'the right of the firstborn' (Deut 21:17), English law gave the eldest the inheritance, and Gouge charges children with their dead parents' 'credit and name.' Even in Korea the heir's work already ran beyond the rites to receiving guests and compiling the genealogy. What is set aside is the heir as sacrificer to the dead: offerings to the dead are forbidden (Deut 26:14), and God may not be worshiped in ways He has not prescribed (WCF 21.1). The urgency that the rites must never cease is set aside with them; Underwood shows it bred such a desire for sons that it justified divorce and concubinage.

rulings.topic: Adopting an heir to continue the sacrifices (立後)
rulings.question: Will we adopt a son into a line that lacks one so that the ancestral sacrifices do not cease?
rulings.practice: If you have no son, adopt an heir from your agnatic kin and charge him to carry on the sacrifices of your line.

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 섭사 攝祀

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 섭사 攝祀

held_by.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, 섭사 攝祀

grounds.citation: Ephesians 1:5
grounds.quote: Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
grounds.point: Scripture makes adoption the very pattern of God's grace, so adoption itself is honorable.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 25:6
grounds.quote: the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel.
grounds.point: God's law itself provides that a sonless line be carried on in name, by succession, not sacrifice.

grounds.citation: Ruth 4:10
grounds.quote: to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren
grounds.point: The name of a dead man is carried on through inheritance and family, with no offering to him.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 26:14
grounds.quote: nor given ought thereof for the dead
grounds.point: An heir charged with offerings to the dead is charged with what Scripture forbids.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 12.1
grounds.quote: by which they are taken into the number, and enjoy the liberties and priviledges of the children of God, have his Name put upon them
grounds.point: Westminster describes adoption as receiving the name and privileges of a son, the model for a family's adoption.

grounds.citation: H. G. Underwood, The Religions of Eastern Asia (1910), Lecture IV, pp. 161-165
grounds.quote: the idea of the necessity that every spirit shall have those who will do him honor and attend to his needs, and that such services can be rendered only by male offspring
grounds.point: Adoption for the rites rests on the belief that the dead need a son to attend to their needs, which is set aside.

rulings.allowed: Adoption is kept. A family may take a child in as a son and heir, give him the family name, inheritance, and place in the register, and so carry on the name and headship of a line that lacks a son. The family's own rules decide whom to adopt. He is charged with the duties of a son and heir to the living family, not with sacrifices.
rulings.resolution: Adoption itself is honored in Scripture, which describes salvation as 'the adoption of children' (Eph 1:5; WCF 12.1), and Scripture provides for continuing a sonless line in its name and inheritance (Deut 25:6; Ruth 4:10) with no sacrifice involved. What is set aside is the purpose this practice gives adoption: an heir charged to keep up offerings to the dead, which Scripture forbids (Deut 26:14). The belief that every spirit must have a son to attend to its needs is what Underwood says produced an inordinate desire for sons; our adoptions serve the living line, not the dead.

rulings.topic: Clan-wide rites for founders and honored ancestors

rulings.practice: Gather the whole clan at the head house each year to offer the great rite to the founding ancestor and the honored, unremoved forebears.

grounds.citation: Psalms 106:28
grounds.quote: They joined themselves also unto Baal-peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead.
grounds.point: Scripture condemns joining in sacrifices made to the dead, which is what the founder's rite is.

grounds.citation: Psalms 78:4
grounds.quote: We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
grounds.point: What the generations gather to tell is God's works among the fathers; this is the kept purpose of a clan gathering.

grounds.citation: Isaiah 63:16
grounds.quote: Doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledge us not
grounds.point: Even the founder of Israel does not know his descendants; God, not the founder, is to be called on.

grounds.citation: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, Chapters 11-12, Section I.12.3
grounds.quote: still the practice was to sacrifice promiscuously to genii and minor gods, or departed heroes: so prone is the descent to this vice of communicating to a crowd that which God strictly claims as his own peculiar right!
grounds.point: Calvin names sacrifice to departed heroes as giving to creatures the worship God claims as his own.

grounds.citation: Resolutions as adopted, I, Records of the China Centenary Missionary Conference (Shanghai, 1907), p. 623
grounds.quote: while the Worship of Ancestors is incompatible with an enlightened and spiritual conception of the Christian Faith, and so cannot be tolerated as a practice in the Christian Church, yet we should be careful to encourage in our Christian converts, the feeling of reverence for the memory of the departed
grounds.point: The conference refused ancestor worship but kept reverence for the memory of the dead.

grounds.citation: W. A. P. Martin, "The Worship of Ancestors: a Plea for Toleration", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 623
grounds.quote: Meeting at the shrine of a common ancestor, the widely severed members are reminded of their blood relationship
grounds.point: Martin defends the clan rites for binding scattered kin together; that good is kept by gathering without the rite.

grounds.citation: E. Faber, discussion, Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 655
grounds.quote: Ancestral worship creates and fosters clannishness, as each clan has its own ancestral protectors; frequent disastrous village wars are the result.
grounds.point: Clan worship treats the founders as protectors, which breeds strife between clans.

grounds.citation: Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture (한국민속대백과사전), 종회 · 내용
grounds.quote: 또한 종회에서는 족보 편찬을 위한 수단사업修單事業을 하고, 서당을 지어 운영하고
grounds.point: The Korean clan assembly also compiles the genealogy and runs schools, which are kept.

rulings.allowed: The clan may gather, at the head house, a hall, or the founder's grave, to meet its kin, read and update the register, tend and mark the graves, tell the founders' history and God's dealings with the family, settle common business, and help its members. The gathering may open and close with prayer to God. No rite, offering, or bow of worship is made to the founder or any ancestor.
rulings.resolution: The clan gathering is kept, because it does what Scripture asks of the generations: to show 'the generation to come the praises of the LORD' (Ps 78:4). Even Martin's plea for toleration praises such meetings because they remind scattered kin of their blood. The great rite to the founder is set aside: it 'ate the sacrifices of the dead' (Ps 106:28), and Calvin names sacrificing to 'departed heroes' as giving away God's peculiar right. Our founders do not know us (Isa 63:16), and the 1907 conference refused the worship but told Christians to keep 'reverence for the memory of the departed.'

rulings.topic: Calling back the soul (皐復)

復衣，不以衣尸，不以斂
復衣，置靈座，恐無妨

grounds.citation: 2 Samuel 12:23
grounds.quote: But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.
grounds.point: David, at his child's death, confesses that the dead cannot be called back.

grounds.citation: Ecclesiastes 12:7
grounds.quote: Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
grounds.point: At death the spirit goes to God, not to a place from which it can be summoned home.

grounds.quote: so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more. He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more.
grounds.point: The dead do not return to their house, which is what the rite calls for.

grounds.point: Westminster teaches that the soul goes immediately to God at death.

grounds.citation: The Second Helvetic Confession, chapters IV, V, XXVI and XXIX, Second Helvetic Confession 26
grounds.quote: For we believe that the faithful, after bodily death, do go directly unto Christ, and, therefore, do not stand in need of helps or prayers for the dead, or any other such duty of them that are alive.
grounds.point: The faithful dead need no ritual service from the living.

grounds.citation: Genesis 23:2
grounds.quote: and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.
grounds.point: Scripture's way at a death is to mourn and weep, and this remains permitted.

grounds.citation: Sangbyeon Tonggo, Mourning Rites, 初終 · 復 (quoting Liji, Tan Gong)
grounds.quote: 復，盡愛之道也，有禱祀之心焉。望返諸幽，求諸鬼神之道也
grounds.point: The rite's own text says it carries the heart of prayer and sacrifice and seeks the soul among the spirits.

rulings.allowed: At a death the family may weep and mourn, close the eyes, cover the body, send for kin and the minister, and pray to God for the living.
rulings.resolution: The calling back of the soul is set aside. Its own commentary admits that it seeks the soul among the spirits with a mind of prayer and sacrifice (復...有禱祀之心焉), but Scripture teaches that the dead do not return ('can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me,' 2 Sam 12:23; Job 7:9-10), and that the spirit returns 'unto God who gave it' (Eccl 12:7; WCF 32.1). The faithful go straight to Christ and need no duty from the living (Second Helvetic 26). Mourning remains, as Abraham came 'to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.'

rulings.topic: Rice and coins in the mouth of the dead (飯含)
rulings.question: Will we place rice and coins in the mouth of the dead?

held_by.citation: Sangbyeon Tonggo, Mourning Rites: death, dressing, encoffining, assuming mournin

grounds.citation: 1 Timothy 6:7
grounds.quote: For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
grounds.point: Nothing can be sent with the dead for their use.

grounds.citation: Psalms 49:17

grounds.point: The dead take nothing with them, so provisions in the mouth serve no one.

grounds.citation: Ecclesiastes 9:5
grounds.quote: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward
grounds.point: The dead have no share in the things of this life, food or coin.

grounds.citation: The Second Helvetic Confession, chapters IV, V, XXVI and XXIX, Second Helvetic Confession 26
grounds.quote: should be honorably, without any superstition, committed to the earth
grounds.point: The Reformed churches bury the body with honor but without superstitious provisions.

grounds.point: Westminster prescribes decent burial without added ceremonies over the body.

grounds.citation: Acts 9:37
grounds.quote: whom when they had washed, they laid her in an upper chamber.
grounds.point: Scripture records washing and laying out the dead; this decent care remains.

grounds.citation: E. Faber, discussion, Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 655
grounds.quote: Ancestral worship presupposes the disembodied souls to be subject to the same desires and wants as souls living in the body.
grounds.point: Provisions for the dead rest on the belief that souls keep the wants of the body.

rulings.allowed: The body may be washed, dressed, and decently laid out and buried according to ordinary custom.
rulings.resolution: Filling the mouth of the dead with rice and coins is set aside. It supposes that the dead keep the wants of the living, but Scripture says 'we can carry nothing out' (1 Tim 6:7), 'when he dieth he shall carry nothing away' (Ps 49:17), and the dead have no more 'a portion for ever in any thing that is done under the sun' (Eccl 9:6). The Reformed churches commit the body to the earth honorably, 'without any superstition,' and enjoin no other care for the dead (Second Helvetic 26; Westminster Directory). Washing and decent preparation remain, as Scripture records them.

rulings.topic: Spirit seat, soul-cloth, and offerings before the body and coffin (靈座, 魂帛, 奠)
rulings.question: Will we set up a spirit seat and soul-cloth for the newly dead and set food, wine, and incense before the body, coffin, and grave during the funeral?
rulings.practice: Set up a spirit seat with a soul-cloth of white silk, and every morning and evening set out food, wine, and incense before it and beside the body as when he was alive.

When the coffin has been let down into the grave, the chief mourner presents the (ruler's) gifts (to the dead in the grave)
He is (supposed to be) grieved at leaving his chamber, and therefore he is brought to the temple of his fathers
The morning offerings should be set forth (beside the body) at sunrise; the evening when the sun is about to set.
With regard to the offerings to the dead at the time of the slighter dressing, Dze-yû said that they should be placed on the east (of the corpse).
When new offerings (of grain or fruits) are presented (beside the body in the coffin), they should be (abundant), like the offerings on the first day of the moon.

held_by.quote: May not what remains in the cupboard suffice to set down (as the offerings) by (the corpse of) one who has just died?

bowing twice, and laying his head to the ground... the mourner again bowed twice and laid his head to the ground

when the ruler withdrew, the rule was that they should then be put down.

靈筵勿設枕幾，朔望祥禫，唯下白粥清水幹棗，不得有酒肉餅果之祭 — At the spirit bier set no pillow or table; on new moon, full moon, and mourning days, offer only white congee, clear water, dried dates; no wine, meat, cakes, fruit.
立喪主...凡主人謂長子無則長孫承重以奉饋奠 — Appoint the chief mourner: the eldest son, or eldest grandson if no son, takes responsibility to perform the offerings.
執事者以卓子置脯醢升自阼階祝盥手洗盞斟酒奠於尸東
結白絹為魂帛置倚上設香爐香合珓杯注酒果於卓子上

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 26:14
grounds.quote: nor given ought thereof for the dead
grounds.point: Setting food and wine before the dead gives part of what is offered to the dead, which Scripture forbids.

grounds.citation: Ecclesiastes 9:5

grounds.point: Offerings made to the dead as if they could receive them contradict Scripture.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Concerning Buriall of the Dead.

grounds.point: Westminster judges religious acts performed toward the corpse superstitious.

grounds.citation: A Directory for the Publique Worship of God, Concerning Buriall of the Dead.
grounds.quote: That this shall not extend to deny any civill respects or differences at the Buriall, suitable to the ranke and condition of the party deceased whiles he was living.
grounds.point: Civil respects at a funeral remain lawful; this is what is permitted.

grounds.citation: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book III, Chapter 5, sections 6-10, Section III.5.10
grounds.quote: Thus, that Christians might not seem worse than heathens, they felt ashamed of paying no office to the dead, as if they had been utterly annihilated. Hence their ill advised assiduity; because they thought they would expose themselves to great disgrace, if they were slow in providing funeral feasts and oblations.
grounds.point: Calvin traces funeral oblations to imitating the heathen, not to Scripture.

grounds.citation: W. A. P. Martin, "The Worship of Ancestors: a Plea for Toleration", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 624
grounds.quote: The souls of the departed are invited to partake of the finer essences of viands destined to supply a feast—a kind of agape—for their living kindred. They are addressed as still retaining consciousness and affection in full measure.
grounds.point: Even the advocate of toleration admits the offerings invite the dead to partake and address them as present.

grounds.citation: Mezzabarba's permissions (1721), quoted in H. Blodget, Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 645
grounds.quote: It is permitted to prepare tables with fruits and viands fit to be eaten, before the tablet or the coffin; provided always that it is done under the aforesaid protest, that everything of a superstitious character be avoided, and that these ceremonies are performed solely in a spirit of gratitude towards the deceased.
grounds.point: The papal legate allowed food before the coffin as gratitude; but food set before the dead is still given to the dead.

grounds.citation: H. Blodget, "The Attitude of Christianity toward Ancestral Worship", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 639
grounds.quote: all prostrations, libations, offerings, prayers, thanksgivings to the dead, whether before the coffin, or in the ancestral hall at the various times for such worship each year, or at the tombs
grounds.point: The 1890 conference paper rejects every offering and prayer to the dead before the coffin.

rulings.allowed: The family may keep watch by the body, mourn, receive and feed living mourners and guests, provide a fitting coffin, and show civil respects at the funeral suited to the person's standing in life, such as standing, bowing the head, and an orderly procession.
rulings.resolution: The spirit seat, the soul-cloth, and the morning and evening offerings before the body are set aside. They serve the dead as though still alive, and Martin himself admits that in such offerings the departed 'are addressed as still retaining consciousness'; Scripture forbids giving 'ought thereof for the dead' (Deut 26:14) and says the dead know nothing (Eccl 9:5). The Westminster Directory calls kneeling and praying 'towards the dead Corps' superstitious, yet keeps 'civill respects' at burial, which is the line we draw. Mezzabarba's 1721 permissions allowed tables of food before the coffin 'in a spirit of gratitude,' but the Protestant missionaries rejected all offerings 'before the coffin,' and Calvin traces funeral oblations to Christians ashamed to seem worse than heathens.

one for the discontented ghosts of his predecessors who had died without posterity

grounds.citation: 2 Samuel 12:23
grounds.quote: But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.
grounds.point: David's response to his child's death is grief and hope, with no service owed to the dead child.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 26:14
grounds.quote: nor given ought thereof for the dead
grounds.point: No offering is to be given to the dead, whether they died old or young.

grounds.citation: Matthew 22:32
grounds.quote: God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.
grounds.point: God is the God of the living, so the dead are not left hungry for want of offerings from their kin.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 32.1
grounds.quote: Beside these two Places, for Souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none.
grounds.point: Scripture leaves no third place where unfed spirits wander.

grounds.citation: E. Faber, discussion, Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 655
grounds.quote: Ancestral worship presupposes that all departed souls, not favored with sacrifices, turn into hungry ghosts and cause all kinds of calamities to the living.
grounds.point: The offerings for the childless dead rest on fear of hungry ghosts.

grounds.citation: H. Blodget, "The Attitude of Christianity toward Ancestral Worship", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 639
grounds.quote: It will teach the decent burial of the poor, of children and of the childless.
grounds.point: The Christian answer is decent burial and a place with the family for the young and childless.

rulings.allowed: Kin who died young or without children are buried with the family, entered in the family register, mourned, and remembered by name like any other member.
rulings.resolution: Offerings for those who died young or without heirs are set aside. They assume that unfed spirits wander and suffer, but Scripture knows only two places for souls after death (WCF 32.1), forbids giving to the dead (Deut 26:14), and David, when his child died, said 'he shall not return to me' and rose to eat. The Protestant missionaries answered this custom with Christian burial of 'children and of the childless,' side by side with the family, and that is what we keep.

rulings.topic: Earth gods, household gods, star-prayers, and charms
rulings.question: Will we offer to the earth god at a grave, keep sacrifices to household gods, pray to the stars, or put star-boards and charms with the dead?
rulings.practice: Before digging a grave, announce to the earth god and offer him wine and food for the peace of the burial place.

Great officers present the oblations of the five sacrifices of the house,--all in the course of the year.
Confucius would stand at the top of his eastern steps, in his court robes, to keep the spirits (of his departed) undisturbed in their shrines.
祠后土於墓左 — Sacrifice to the earth god at the left of the grave.

grounds.citation: Matthew 4:10
grounds.quote: Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
grounds.point: Worship belongs to God alone, not to an earth god or a household god.

grounds.citation: 1 Corinthians 10:20
grounds.quote: But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils.
grounds.point: Offerings to the gods of the land and house are offerings to devils.

grounds.citation: Psalms 24:1
grounds.quote: The earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof
grounds.point: The burial ground belongs to the LORD, not to an earth god who must be appeased.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 4:19
grounds.quote: And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them
grounds.point: Scripture forbids prayers to the stars and reverence for the Dipper as ruler of life and death.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 18:11
grounds.quote: Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer.
grounds.point: Charms are named among the abominations God forbids.

grounds.citation: The Larger Catechism, WLC 113
grounds.quote: the creatures or any thing contained under the name of God, to charms
grounds.point: Westminster counts the use of charms a sin against the third commandment.

grounds.citation: The Cathechisme or manner how to instruct and teach children and others in the C, HC 94
grounds.quote: Sorcerie, Enchauntmentes, superstition or worshipping of God, by other meanes then hee hath taught in his worde
grounds.point: The Heidelberg Catechism forbids sorcery, enchantments, and superstition under the first commandment.

grounds.citation: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, Chapters 11-12, Section I.12.3
grounds.quote: still the practice was to sacrifice promiscuously to genii and minor gods, or departed heroes
grounds.point: Calvin condemns sacrifice to minor gods and spirits of place.

rulings.allowed: The family asks God alone, in its own prayers, for the peace of the house, the health of its members, and a safe burial, and gives Him thanks. Graves may be dug and coffins made by ordinary craft, with no charm or star-board.
rulings.resolution: Offerings to the earth god and household gods, prayers to the stars, and charms are all set aside. 'The earth is the LORD's' (Ps 24:1), worship is His alone (Matt 4:10), and what is sacrificed to such powers is sacrificed 'to devils, and not to God' (1 Cor 10:20). Scripture forbids worshiping 'the host of heaven' and forbids charmers (Deut 4:19; 18:11), and the Westminster and Heidelberg Catechisms count charms and sorcery as sins against God's name and worship. Calvin names sacrifice to 'genii and minor gods' as giving God's right to creatures.

grounds.quote: It will enjoin also interment at the proper time, without regard to the superstitions of geomancy and divination for lucky days
grounds.point: The Christian rule is timely burial without regard to geomancy.

grounds.citation: Sima Guang, Jia Fan 5 (子下) 29

grounds.citation: Yi I, Haeju Community Compact, faults of not rejecting heterodoxy (不斥異端)

rulings.allowed: Choose a grave by ordinary reasons: a family plot near kin, lawful purchase or ownership, a sound and accessible site, and the wishes of the dead. Bury at the proper time, and move a grave only for practical necessity, never for fortune.
rulings.resolution: Divining a grave site and geomancy are set aside. Scripture forbids diviners and observers of times (Deut 18:10-14), and the patriarchs chose their burying place by kinship and lawful purchase (Gen 49:31). To expect wealth, rank, or long life from a grave's position is 'ascribing the praise of any good ... to fortune' (WLC 105). Even within the tradition, Sima Guang held that burial cannot change one's lot, and Yi I's Haeju compact counted it a fault to move ancestral graves on geomancers' advice.
