held_by.citation: Sangbyeon Tonggo, Capping and Marriage Rites, 納采
held_by.quote: 將以加諸卜筮。 — We will submit it to divination.

held_by.citation: Sangbyeon Tonggo, 6 Nacai: Shizhe fuming, Xushi fugao yu citang, Naji
held_by.quote: 歸卜於廟，得吉兆 — Return to the temple to divine, obtain an auspicious omen.

held_by.citation: Sangbyeon Tonggo, 6 Nacai: Shizhe fuming, Xushi fugao yu citang, Naji
held_by.quote: 吾子有貺命，某加諸卜，占曰吉，使某也，敢告 — You gave a command; I added divination; the oracle says auspicious; I am sent to tell you.

grounds.citation: Deuteronomy 18:10
grounds.quote: that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch
grounds.point: Scripture forbids both divination and observing times for good or ill fortune.

grounds.citation: Leviticus 19:26
grounds.quote: neither shall ye use enchantment, nor observe times.
grounds.point: God's law forbids choosing lucky and unlucky times.

grounds.citation: Galatians 4:10–11
grounds.quote: Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years. I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain.
grounds.point: Paul treats the observance of days and seasons as a return to bondage.

grounds.citation: Isaiah 47:13
grounds.quote: Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee.
grounds.point: God mocks those who trust astrologers and month-readers to secure their future.

grounds.citation: James 4:15
grounds.quote: For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
grounds.point: Christians make plans by committing them to God's will, not by reading omens.

grounds.citation: Proverbs 16:33
grounds.quote: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
grounds.point: Scripture allows the lot as an appeal to God's disposing, which some take to permit divination; it is not the reading of auspicious days or omens.

grounds.citation: The Cathechisme or manner how to instruct and teach children and others in the C, HC 94
grounds.quote: Sorcerie, Enchauntmentes, superstition or worshipping of God, by other meanes then hee hath taught in his worde
grounds.point: The Heidelberg Catechism forbids sorcery and superstition under the first commandment.

grounds.citation: H. Blodget, "The Attitude of Christianity toward Ancestral Worship", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 651
grounds.quote: The bare mention of the dark ways of the doctors of geomancy, the diviners for lucky days, the manifold tricks of Buddhist and Taoist priests
grounds.point: The 1890 conference paper counts diviners of lucky days among the evils Christians are delivered from.

rulings.allowed: Dates for weddings, coming-of-age, and funerals are set by convenience, the readiness of the persons, and the church's calendar, and every plan is committed to God in prayer: 'If the Lord will.'
rulings.resolution: Casting the tortoise-shell or stalks, choosing lucky days, and divining before the ancestors are set aside. God forbids 'divination' and the 'observer of times' (Deut 18:10; Lev 19:26), Paul rebukes those who 'observe days, and months, and times, and years' (Gal 4:10), and the astrologers 'shall be as stubble' (Isa 47:13-14). Scripture does record the lot, but as leaving 'the whole disposing' to the LORD (Prov 16:33), not as reading auspicious omens; the Heidelberg Catechism forbids sorcery and superstition, and the 1890 conference counted 'the diviners for lucky days' as part of the bondage Christians are freed from. We plan and say, 'If the Lord will.'

rulings.topic: Prayers, masses, alms, and religious merit for the souls of the dead
rulings.question: Will we pray, have masses said, give alms, or make Buddhist offerings for the good of a dead relative's soul?
rulings.practice: Pray for your deceased family members and expend part of their estate in pious works for the good of their souls.

held_by.citation: Gratissimam Sane, I · THE CIVILIZATION OF LOVE · 10 · The common good of marriage and the family
held_by.quote: In prayer everyone should be present: the living and those who have died, and also those yet to come into the world.

held_by.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, bk. II, ch. VI, § 4 (Intestacy)
held_by.quote: his chattels shall be distributed by the hands of his next kinsfolk and friends under the supervision of the church
when he does make a residuary gift, he frequently makes it in favour of his executors and bids them expend it for his benefit
The dead's part they are to distribute for the good of his soul in such pious works as they shall think best according to God and good conscience.
procure Diriges, Masses, Pardons, Releases... make continuall prayers to free them out of Purgatory

四時祭祀，周、孔所教...若報罔極之德，霜露之悲，有時齋供，及七月半盂蘭盆，望於汝也 — Seasonal sacrifices are taught by Zhou and Confucius... to repay boundless virtue, at times make vegetarian offerings and mid-seventh-month Ullambana; I look to you.
Much might be done by a pious heir for the good of his ancestor’s soul, and the duty of doing this was sedulously preached

held_by.citation: History of English Law, Book II, Ch. VII, § 2
held_by.quote: When the wife dies intestate, ought one-third, or perhaps one-half, of the chattels to be distributed for the good of her soul?

grounds.citation: Hebrews 9:27
grounds.quote: And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment
grounds.point: The state of the dead is settled at death, so nothing done by the living alters it.

grounds.citation: The Humble Advice of the Assembly of Divines ... Concerning a Confession of Fait, WCF 21.4
grounds.quote: Prayer is to be made for things lawful, and for all sorts of men living, or that shall live hereafter: but, not for the Dead
grounds.point: Westminster limits prayer to the living and those yet to live.

grounds.citation: The Thirty-nine Articles of Religion, Article XXII, standard English text
grounds.quote: The Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory, Pardons, Worshipping and Adoration, as well of Images as of Relics, and also Invocation of Saints, is a fond thing, vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture, but rather repugnant to the Word of God.
grounds.point: The Articles reject purgatory and pardons, the basis of masses and alms for souls.

grounds.citation: An Homilee or Sermon concerning Prayer, three parts, including the question of p, The third part (part 3)
grounds.quote: Let vs not therfore dreame either of purgatorie, or of prayer for the soules of them that be dead: but let vs earnestly & diligently praye for them whiche are expresly commaunded in holye scripture
grounds.point: The Homily turns prayer away from the dead to those Scripture commands us to pray for.

grounds.citation: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book III, Chapter 5, sections 6-10, Section III.5.10
grounds.quote: But far better and more solid comfort is furnished by scripture when it declares, “Blessed are the dead that die in the Lord;” and adds the reason, “for they rest from their labors,” (Rev. 14:13). We ought not to indulge our love so far as to set up a perverse mode of prayer in the Church.
grounds.point: Calvin answers the love that prompts prayer for the dead: the dead in Christ rest, and love may not invent a form of prayer.

grounds.citation: The Second Helvetic Confession, chapters IV, V, XXVI and XXIX, Second Helvetic Confession 26
grounds.quote: we should make honorable mention of those who died in the Lord, and perform all duties of love to those they leave behind, as their widows and fatherless children. Other care for the dead we do not enjoin.
grounds.point: The Reformed duty to the dead is honorable mention and care for their survivors, nothing more.

grounds.citation: Gratissimam Sane, The common good of marriage and the family
grounds.quote: In prayer everyone should be present: the living and those who have died, and also those yet to come into the world. Families should pray for all of their members
grounds.point: Rome asks the family to pray for its dead members; answered by Scripture's silence and the Westminster limit to the living.

grounds.citation: W. A. P. Martin, "The Worship of Ancestors: a Plea for Toleration", Records of the General Conference of the Protestant Missionaries of China (Shanghai, 1890), p. 628
grounds.quote: Far more humane is the Catholic custom of keeping alive their affections by praying for the dead.
grounds.point: A Protestant missionary admired prayer for the dead as humane; Calvin answers that love may not set up a prayer God has not commanded.

rulings.allowed: Give thanks to God for the faithful departed and their example; speak of them with honor; care for the widows and children they leave behind; and give to the church, the poor, or a school in their memory for the good of the living. Wills and bequests to charity are carried out as ordinary gifts, not as payments for a soul.
rulings.resolution: Prayers, masses, alms, and Buddhist offerings for the souls of the dead are set aside. After death comes judgment (Heb 9:27); prayer is for the living, 'not for the Dead' (WCF 21.4); purgatory is 'a fond thing, vainly invented' (Article 22); and the Homily tells us not to 'dreame ... of prayer for the soules of them that be dead.' Gratissimam Sane asks families to pray for 'those who have died,' and Martin confessed he would like to; Calvin answers that 'we ought not to indulge our love so far as to set up a perverse mode of prayer,' since the dead in the Lord already 'rest from their labors.' What remains is what the Second Helvetic Confession enjoins: honorable mention of the dead and duties of love to those they leave behind.

rulings.topic: Invoking Mary and the saints
rulings.question: Will we pray to the Virgin Mary and the saints, say the rosary, and visit Marian shrines?
rulings.practice: Implore the help of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the saints, pray the family rosary together, and visit her shrines.

held_by.quote: implore the help of the Blessed and Immaculate Virgin Mary... ask the princes of the Apostles, Peter and Paul... to save the human race by their powerful patronage.
invoke the aid of the Blessed Virgin and the saints... Do you say the family rosary together?
the rosary should be considered as one of the best and most efficacious prayers in common that the Christian family is invited to recite
she who is the Mother of Christ and of the Church is in a special way the Mother of Christian families, of domestic Churches
visit Marian shrines and gaze upon the face of the Mother of God

grounds.citation: 1 Timothy 2:5
grounds.quote: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus
grounds.point: Christ alone mediates between God and men, so no saint is to be called on as intercessor.

grounds.citation: Luke 1:48
grounds.quote: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.
grounds.point: Scripture honors Mary as blessed in every generation; this honor is kept, but it is not invocation.

grounds.citation: The Larger Catechism, WLC 105
grounds.quote: praying, or giving any religious worship to Saints, Angels, or any other creatures
grounds.point: Westminster lists prayer to saints among the sins against the first commandment.

grounds.citation: The Thirty-nine Articles of Religion, Article XXII, standard English text
grounds.quote: and also Invocation of Saints, is a fond thing, vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture, but rather repugnant to the Word of God.
grounds.point: The Articles reject the invocation of saints as without warrant in Scripture.

grounds.citation: The Second Helvetic Confession, chapters IV, V, XXVI and XXIX, Second Helvetic Confession 5
grounds.quote: we do neither adore, worship, nor pray unto the saints in heaven, or to other gods; neither do we acknowledge them for our intercessors or mediators before the Father in heaven.
grounds.point: The Second Helvetic Confession refuses prayer to the saints and their mediation.

grounds.citation: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Section III.20.21
grounds.quote: it were the extreme of stupidity, not to say madness, to attempt to obtain access by means of others, so as to be drawn away from him without whom access cannot be obtained.
grounds.point: Calvin: seeking God through the saints draws us away from Christ, the only access.

grounds.citation: An Homilee or Sermon concerning Prayer, three parts, including the question of p, The second part (part 2)
grounds.quote: His mynde therefore is this, not that we shoulde put any religion in worshyppyng them, or praying vnto them: but that we shoulde honour them by folowyng their vertuous and godly lyfe.
grounds.point: The Homily keeps honor for the saints through imitation, not prayer.

grounds.citation: Familiaris Consortio, 60 · Educators in Prayer
grounds.quote: Do you encourage them when they are sick to think of Christ suffering to invoke the aid of the Blessed Virgin and the saints Do you say the family rosary together?
grounds.point: Rome urges families to invoke the Virgin and saints and say the rosary; answered by Christ's sole mediation.

rulings.allowed: Call Mary blessed, as Scripture does, and honor her and the saints by learning from and imitating their faith. The family prays together, often and aloud, to God alone through Christ.
rulings.resolution: Invoking Mary and the saints, the rosary's prayers to Mary, and pilgrimages to her shrines are set aside. There is 'one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus' (1 Tim 2:5); Westminster forbids 'praying, or giving any religious worship to Saints'; Article 22 calls invocation of saints 'a fond thing'; and the Second Helvetic Confession does not 'pray unto the saints' or count them intercessors. Calvin calls seeking access by others 'the extreme of stupidity'. Familiaris Consortio urges families to invoke the Virgin and the saints and say the rosary, but Scripture's honor of Mary is that 'all generations shall call me blessed' (Luke 1:48), and the Homily teaches that we honor the saints by following their godly life, not by praying to them.

rulings.topic: Keep affection between father and child; do not let rank freeze it.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Confucian · Mencius 3A:4 (父子有親)).
rulings.practice: Keep affection between father and child; do not let rank freeze it.

grounds.citation: Baxter, The Poor Man's Family Book, Counsel to Reforming Fathers
grounds.quote: make them not so familiar with you as shall breed contempt, and be not so strange to them as shall tempt them to have no love to you
grounds.point: Do all that you do with them in love and wisdom, avoiding too much familiarity that breeds contempt and too much strangeness that hinders love, so they perceive your tender fatherly care is for their good.

grounds.citation: Baxter, Leading a Family for Christ
grounds.quote: If you make your children... your playfellows or equals... they will scorn to be subject where they have once been as equal.
grounds.point: Do not make your children your playfellows or equals; keep your place as governor, lest they scorn to be subject where they have once been equal.

grounds.citation: Richard Baxter, in Una teología de la familia, Dirigir a una familia para Cristo
grounds.quote: No pierdas tu autoridad por conceder demasiada familiaridad. Si conviertes a tus hijos... en tus compañeros de juego o en tus iguales, y les hablas y les permites que te hablen como colegas
grounds.point: Do not lose your authority by excessive familiarity; do not make your children your playmates or equals or allow them to speak as colleagues.

grounds.citation: Richard Baxter, in Una teología de la familia, PDF p. 284
grounds.quote: No les permitas tanta familiaridad contigo que pueda producir desprecio y tampoco seas tan distante de ellos como para tentarlos a no amarte... Deja que perciban el tierno corazón de un padre — Do not allow so much familiarity with you as to breed contempt, nor be so distant as to tempt them not …
grounds.point: Treat your children with love and wisdom: avoid excessive familiarity that breeds contempt and excessive distance that hinders love; let them feel your tender heart and see that your counsel is for their good.

rulings.resolution: Puritan and Reformed sources (Baxter's directions, repeated in the modern Reformed manuals) warn against both errors: so much familiarity that children make the father their playfellow and equal and come to scorn his rule, and so much distance that love is hindered. Duty 26 warns only against coldness. Yen Family Instructions and Puritan counsel join tenderness with dignity: relations between parents and children should be 'dignified without familiarity', lest love turn to rudeness; the duty warns only against rank freezing affection.
rulings.revision: Keep warm affection between father and child, but keep your place: be neither so distant that it hinders love nor so familiar that it breeds contempt.

rulings.topic: Once they marry, counsel when asked and let the new house govern itself.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Our house · Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol II).
rulings.practice: Once they marry, counsel when asked and let the new house govern itself.

held_by.citation: Covenant Home: Parental Honoring Protocol II

grounds.citation: John Angell James, in Biblical Parenthood, Principle Obstacles in Bringing Up Children for Christ
grounds.quote: as long as children continue beneath the parental roof, they are to be subject to the rules of domestic discipline
grounds.point: Continue to exercise parental discipline over your children as long as they remain in your home; do not give up authority too early.

grounds.citation: James, Una teología de la familia, Advertencia a los jóvenes sobre el pecado
grounds.quote: los padres hayan rebajado el rigor de la disciplina doméstica porque piensen que sus hijos han aumentado en saber y que, por lo tanto, se merecen el halago.
grounds.point: Do not relax discipline over your children just because they have become more educated; they still need it.

grounds.citation: Patriarchalism in Political Thought, p. 266
grounds.quote: The father’s ‘power of Commanding ends with Nonage’... when he comes to that Estate that made his Father a Freeman, the Son is a Freeman too
grounds.point: End your command over your child when he reaches the age of discretion and reason; he becomes a freeman as his father was.

grounds.citation: Demos, A Little Commonwealth, Parents and Children
grounds.quote: a parent would normally continue to concern himself directly in the personal affairs of his children, even when they had become adult and were involved with families of their own.
grounds.point: Continue to concern yourself directly in the personal affairs of your children, even when they are adult and have families of their own.

grounds.citation: Ancestor Worship and Korean Society, Families of the Twisongdwi Lineage
grounds.quote: After reaching the age of 60, both men and women are expected to begin passing on the responsibilities of farm and household management to the succeeding generation.
grounds.point: Upon reaching sixty, begin passing on the responsibilities of farm and household management to the succeeding generation.

grounds.citation: Ancestor Worship and Korean Society, Families of the Twisongdwi Lineage
grounds.quote: elders should not interfere too greatly in day-to-day decision making.
grounds.point: Do not interfere too greatly in day-to-day decision making once authority is passed on.

rulings.resolution: Puritan sources keep parental discipline in force while children live under the parental roof, and Locke (via Schochet) ends the power of command at the age of discretion; Korean elders hand over management around sixty and then do not interfere; English custom sets children up in their own household at marriage, though New England parents kept a hand in adult children's affairs. The release turns on coming of age and leaving the roof, not on marriage alone.
rulings.revision: While they live under your roof, keep your authority; once they come of age and set up their own house, by marriage or otherwise, counsel when asked and let that house govern itself.

rulings.topic: Marry with your parents' knowledge and blessing sought, not behind their backs.
rulings.question: The newly read books show the wording of this duty (Our house · Our house).
rulings.practice: Marry with your parents' knowledge and blessing sought, not behind their backs.

grounds.citation: John Angell James, in Una teología de la familia, Pensamientos sobre cómo encontrar pareja matrimonial
grounds.quote: Pero hasta que seas mayor de edad, tienen la autoridad de prohibirte — but until you are of age, they have authority to forbid you.
grounds.point: If you are under age, obey your parents when they forbid you from pursuing a relationship.

grounds.citation: The Duties of Children and Parents, I.A (Obedience proper 3)
grounds.quote: In your choice of a spouse. Parents should “sway much” in this matter.
grounds.point: In choosing a spouse, let your parents guide you; do not marry without their consent; if they choose someone you cannot love, humbly persuade them; refuse only if they choose an ungodly partner.

grounds.citation: Thomas Watson, in Una teología de la familia, Honra a tu padre y a tu madre
grounds.quote: Jacob no se iba a casar, aunque ya tenía cuarenta años, sin la aprobación de sus padres — Jacob was not going to marry, though he was forty years old, without his parents' approval.
grounds.point: Do not marry without your parents' approval.

grounds.citation: Family and Inheritance: Rural Society in Western Europe, 1200-1800, pp. 261-262
grounds.quote: sons under the age of twenty-five as well as daughters could be disinherited for marrying without their father’s consent.
grounds.point: Do not marry without your father's consent, or he may disinherit you.

grounds.citation: English Villagers of the Thirteenth Century, pp. 172-174
grounds.quote: First, a man could not marry without his father's consent.
grounds.point: Do not marry without your father's consent.

grounds.citation: Marriage Ring, Be guided by the advice of parents or guardians
grounds.quote: it is a violation of your duty to them to form connections without their knowledge and to maintain them against their prohibitions.
grounds.point: While under age, do not form connections without their knowledge or maintain them against their prohibitions.

grounds.citation: Marriage Ring, Be guided by the advice of parents or guardians
grounds.quote: parents rest their objections on sufficient grounds and show plain reasons for prohibiting a marriage, it is the plain duty of sons, and especially of daughters, to give it up.
grounds.point: If your parents have sufficient grounds and plain reasons, give up the intended marriage.

grounds.citation: Family and Inheritance, Inheritance and settlement by great landowners 265
grounds.quote: sons under the age of thirty and of daughters under twenty-five, on pain of total disinheritance
grounds.point: Obtain your parents' consent before marrying if you are under thirty, on pain of total disinheritance.

rulings.resolution: Puritan, English and colonial sources (Gouge-style duties, The Marriage Ring, Plymouth and Andover records, English custom) require parents' consent, not merely their knowledge and blessing, for a child under their authority, and teach giving up a match they oppose on sound grounds; the clan wording understates this.
rulings.revision: Marry with your parents' consent, not behind their backs: while under their authority do not court or marry without it, and give up a match they oppose for sound reasons.

rulings.topic: Share the care of parents; do not leave it to one.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Our house · Our house).
rulings.practice: Share the care of parents; do not leave it to one.

grounds.citation: Family and Property, The Harmony of Co-Residents
grounds.quote: let their parents go hungry or remain unburied rather than do more than another brother could or would do (1.35)
grounds.point: Do not let your parents go hungry or remain unburied because you are unwilling to do more than your siblings.

grounds.citation: Yüan Ts'ai, Precepts 1.35
grounds.quote: There are brothers who will insist that all of them share equally in supporting their parents, even though one is poor, preferring to see the parents neglected
grounds.point: Support your parents even if your brothers are poor; do not insist that all share equally, but do extra yourself out of sympathy.

grounds.citation: Yüan Ts'ai, Precepts 1.35
grounds.quote: Some brothers would rather see their parents left unburied than make an exception to the principle of all contributing equally, out of sympathy for one brother's poverty.
grounds.point: Bury your parents even if your brothers cannot contribute equally; make an exception to the principle of equal contribution out of sympathy for a brother's poverty.

rulings.resolution: Yuan Ts'ai condemns brothers who leave parents hungry or unburied rather than do more than a poorer brother can; sharing must not become a reason to hold back.
rulings.revision: Share the care of parents; do not leave it to one, and do not hold back your own part because a poorer brother cannot match it.

rulings.topic: Keep the record of the family and gather it at the appointed times.
rulings.question: The newly read books show the wording of this duty (Korean custom · 족보 (jokbo)).
rulings.practice: Keep the record of the family and gather it at the appointed times.

grounds.citation: Lineage Organization in Southeastern China, PDF p. 80
grounds.quote: It was revised, or at least it was supposed to be revised, about every one or two generations
grounds.point: See that the genealogy is revised every one or two generations, adding marriages, births, and deaths.

grounds.citation: Korean Women: View from the Inner Room, Early Genealogies
grounds.quote: both record sons and daughters in order of birth, not sons first and daughters last.
grounds.point: Record your sons and daughters in the genealogy in their order of birth, not sons first and daughters last.

grounds.citation: Korean Women: View from the Inner Room, Early Genealogies
grounds.quote: lines of descent of daughters as well as those of sons are recorded continuously — through their sons and daughters and grandsons and granddaughters
grounds.point: Record the descendants of your daughters through their sons and daughters and grandchildren as continuously as the male line.

rulings.resolution: The sources describe keeping and revising the written genealogy each generation, with births, marriages and deaths, and early Korean genealogies record daughters and their descendants in birth order alongside sons; 'gather it at the appointed times' is not what they describe and leans toward the calendar.
rulings.revision: Keep the family's written record and revise it each generation, entering sons and daughters alike with their births, marriages and deaths.

rulings.topic: Make her husband's house her own: his parents and kin are now hers to honor.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Korean custom · 출가 (出嫁); 시댁).
rulings.practice: Make her husband's house her own: his parents and kin are now hers to honor.

grounds.citation: Lineage Organization in Southeastern China, PDF p. 144-145
grounds.quote: the married woman was forced to cast her interests fully within the group of which she was a member by marriage
grounds.point: Cast your interests fully with your husband's lineage, and do not keep ties to your natal kin.

grounds.citation: Lineage Organization in Southeastern China, PDF p. 32
grounds.quote: the Chinese system of marriage identified the interests of a married woman strongly with those of her new family and severed her formal economic ties with her natal family
grounds.point: Let your interests be identified with your husband's family, and sever formal economic ties with your natal family.

grounds.citation: The Confucian Transformation of Korea, Life in the Husband's Household
grounds.quote: The descent group into which she married took precedence at all times over the family she had started or was about to start.
grounds.point: Submit to your husband's descent group and place it above the family you have started.

rulings.resolution: Deuchler and Freedman report that in Korea and China joining the husband's house meant ranking his descent group above the family the wife herself was starting, and cutting her economic ties with her own kin. That conflicts with leave-and-cleave [300] and [56] and with honoring her own parents [158]; the duty should not carry it.
rulings.revision: Make her husband's kin her own to honor, while keeping faith with her own parents and putting her marriage and their own household first.

rulings.topic: Obey while living at home; when grown, obedience ends but respect does not.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Catholic · CCC 2217).
rulings.practice: Obey while living at home; when grown, obedience ends but respect does not.

grounds.citation: John Angell James, in Godly Manhood, Threats to Godliness in Young Men
grounds.quote: look up to his parents as his counselors, his comforters, and, in some respects, his rulers
grounds.point: Look up to your parents as your counselors, comforters, and in some respects rulers; allow the restraints of home to follow you abroad.

grounds.citation: John Angell James, in Godly Manhood, Threats to Godliness in Young Men
grounds.quote: Paternal rule is now over; my parents are not at hand to be consulted or obeyed; and if they were, it is time for me to think and act for myself.
grounds.point: Do not think that parental rule is over when you leave home; still honor your parents' counsel and do not set yourself up as your own master.

grounds.citation: John Angell James, in Una teología de la familia, Capítulo 2—Hombres piadosos, PDF p. 99
grounds.quote: considera un privilegio y su deber considerar a sus padres como sus consejeros, sus alentadores y, en algunos sentidos, sus tutores.
grounds.point: After leaving your father's house and reaching maturity, still regard it as a privilege and duty to treat your parents as your counselors, encouragers, and in some ways guardians.

grounds.citation: Demos, A Little Commonwealth, Parents and Children
grounds.quote: the child owed his parents an unceasing kind of obedience and respect
grounds.point: Give your parents unceasing obedience and respect, and listen to their counsel even as an adult.

grounds.citation: Pink, Fatherhood: Responsibility and Privilege
grounds.quote: disobedience on the part of children to their parents during the days of childhood and their lack of reverence and respect when they grow up.
grounds.point: Obey your parents and show them reverence and respect both in childhood and adulthood.

rulings.resolution: Pink, J. A. James and Demos's Plymouth evidence say grown children still treat parents as counselors and 'in some respects rulers,' and keep obedience and reverence into adulthood; 'obedience ends' is too absolute.
rulings.revision: Obey while living at home; when grown and gone, still treat them as your counselors, heed their lawful wishes, and never stop honoring them.

rulings.topic: Be a good younger brother or sister: yield and follow; it is the root of humaneness.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Confucian · Analects 1:2 (孝弟 為仁之本)).
rulings.practice: Be a good younger brother or sister: yield and follow; it is the root of humaneness.

grounds.citation: John Angell James, in Una teología de la familia, Capítulo 12
grounds.quote: que este modelo no sea solamente el objeto de su atención y admiración, sino de su imitación — let this model be not only the object of their attention and admiration, but of their imitation.
grounds.point: Imitate the good example of your older siblings; if their conduct is evil, do not follow it, and resist any threat, bribe, or argument to do wrong.

rulings.resolution: Una teologia de la familia (Modern Reformed, which outranks Confucian) tells younger siblings to imitate their elders' good example, but if the elders' conduct is evil, not to follow it and to resist any threat, bribe or argument to do wrong. The duty's bare 'yield and follow' sets no limit.
rulings.revision: Be a good younger brother or sister: yield to your elders and follow them in what is good, but do not follow an elder sibling into wrong, whatever he threatens, offers or argues.

rulings.topic: Seek a worthy marriage for the widows and the unmarried in his keeping.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Scripture · Ruth 3:1; 4:13; Gen 24).
rulings.practice: Seek a worthy marriage for the widows and the unmarried in his keeping.

grounds.citation: Kinship Organization in Late Imperial China, 1000-1940, Marriage, Adoption, and Charity
grounds.quote: would not be forced to remarry or produce her own income should her husband die
grounds.point: Do not force a widow to remarry or to earn her own income; provide for her needs from the lineage estate.

grounds.citation: Kinship Organization in Late Imperial China, MARRIAGE, ADOPTION, AND CHARITY
grounds.quote: women were assured of not being forced to remarry should their husbands die without sons
grounds.point: Do not force a widow to remarry even if her husband died without a son.

grounds.citation: Kinship Organization in Late Imperial China, 1000-1940, PDF pp. 403-407
grounds.quote: the widow might be forced to remarry (thereby losing any claim to the estate)
grounds.point: Do not force a widow to remarry and lose her claim to her husband's estate.

grounds.citation: The Confucian Transformation of Korea, Notes to pp. 279-290
grounds.quote: Officially the Kabo reforms of 1894 ended the widow's predicament by ruling that widows of any social class were henceforth free to remarry.
grounds.point: Leave a widow free to remarry; do not hinder her.

rulings.resolution: Chinese lineage rules (Ebrey/Watson) protected widows from being forced to remarry or to earn their own keep, and the 1894 Korean reform left widows free to remarry. The duty tells the acting head to seek a marriage for widows, but says nothing of her consent or of her keep if she declines.
rulings.revision: Help the widows and the unmarried in his keeping toward a worthy marriage if they wish it; never force a widow to remarry or hinder her, and do not make her keep or her share of her husband's estate depend on it.

rulings.topic: At a funeral, bow to the mourners and comfort them; stand in silence before the dead rather than bow to them.
rulings.question: The newly read books show the wording of this duty (Our house · Our house).
rulings.practice: At a funeral, bow to the mourners and comfort them; stand in silence before the dead rather than bow to them.
rulings.resolution: Korean custom confirms that callers bow to the chief mourner and comfort the family, but it adds a bow to the dead once the body is dressed, as a new ancestor. That bow is the point where the house departs, on the ground of [247]. The duty should name the chief mourner and say plainly where it parts from custom.
rulings.revision: At a funeral, bow to the chief mourner and the family and comfort them; where custom turns to bowing before the dead, stand in silence instead.

rulings.topic: Mourn your adoptive parents as a natural child mourns his own.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Korean custom · Daejeon Hoetong, 五服 6).
rulings.practice: Mourn your adoptive parents as a natural child mourns his own.

grounds.citation: Mourning in Late Imperial China, PDF p. 140-141
grounds.quote: For their natural parents they could receive a maximum leave of up to one year to superintend the burial (zhisang), if they so desired
grounds.point: Limit mourning for your natural parents to at most one year for their burial, rather than the full twenty-seven months.

grounds.citation: Korean Adoption and Inheritance, PDF p. 99-101
grounds.quote: and only mourns one year for his natural parents.
grounds.point: Mourn your natural parents for one year, as required for one adopted out.

rulings.resolution: Korean and Qing rules have the adopted heir mourn his adoptive parents in full but still mourn his birth parents, one grade lower (one year); the duty says nothing of the parents who bore him.
rulings.revision: Mourn your adoptive parents as a natural child mourns his own, and still mourn the parents who bore you.

rulings.topic: Where a house has no son to carry it on, see that an heir is rightly adopted from the kin, with the family's knowledge and witness.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Confucian · Jia Fan, 8.10).
rulings.practice: Where a house has no son to carry it on, see that an heir is rightly adopted from the kin, with the family's knowledge and witness.

grounds.citation: The Confucian Transformation of Korea, PDF p. 174-176
grounds.quote: reluctant to designate an heir for her late husband
grounds.point: Designate an heir for your late husband to continue his line.

grounds.citation: The Confucian Transformation of Korea, PDF p. 174-176
grounds.quote: disregarded her spouse's last will
grounds.point: Honor your late husband's last will in choosing an heir.

grounds.citation: Peterson, Korean Women: View from the Inner Room, pp. 34-35
grounds.quote: the responsibility for providing an adopted son for a man who had died without issue was transferred from his widow to representatives of the lineage
grounds.point: Arrange for a son to be adopted for a man who died without issue, so his line may continue.

grounds.citation: Korean Women, pp. 54-55
grounds.quote: requests for adoptions initiated by lineage representatives, ignoring the role of the wife, increased in frequency and became routine
grounds.point: When a couple dies without an heir, arrange an adoption to continue their line.

rulings.resolution: Deuchler reports that the widow of a sonless heir was bound to name an heir for him and to follow his last will in the choice; Peterson shows the right passing from the widow to lineage representatives who ignored her. The duty leaves out the dead man's own wishes and his widow's voice.
rulings.revision: Where a house has no son to carry it on, see that an heir is rightly adopted from the near kin, following the dead man's own wishes and hearing his widow, with the family's knowledge and witness.

rulings.topic: Pay the funeral charges and debts of the dead, and make good his pledges, before anyone takes an inheritance.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Puritan · Gouge, Domesticall Duties 5.47).
rulings.practice: Pay the funeral charges and debts of the dead, and make good his pledges, before anyone takes an inheritance.

grounds.citation: Property and Kinship, Families, Creditors, and Neighbors: Estate Administration
grounds.quote: Widows did have claim to small amounts of personal property unreachable by estate holders’ creditors.
grounds.point: Set aside for the widow her necessaries and dower before creditors and heirs take the estate.

grounds.citation: Property and Kinship, Appendix B
grounds.quote: the courts were required to exempt certain personal property from creditor claims
grounds.point: See that the widow keeps household necessities free from the claims of creditors.

grounds.citation: Women and the Law of Property, PDF pp. 184-185
grounds.quote: executors or administrators used personal property first to meet the demands of creditors... the widow received her life interest before real property was attached to pay debts
grounds.point: Use the personal estate first to pay the husband's debts, and do not let creditors take the widow's dower real property during her lifetime.

grounds.citation: Women and the Law of Property in Early America, Conclusion (PDF p. 208-209)
grounds.quote: widows’ liens on family property and lifetime shares in insolvent estates
grounds.point: Honor the widow's lien on family property and give her a lifetime share even when the estate is insolvent.

grounds.citation: Women and the Law of Property in Early America, PDF p. 252-253
grounds.quote: the widow's dower is preferred to heirs or creditors
grounds.point: Prefer a widow's dower claim over those of heirs and creditors.

grounds.citation: Women and the Law of Property in Early America, PDF p. 252-253
grounds.quote: to allow women this prior claim
grounds.point: Give women their claim before other creditors when an estate is insolvent.

grounds.citation: Women and the Law of Property in Early America, PDF pp. 247-248
grounds.quote: the widows of insolvents usually kept bedding and cooking utensils
grounds.point: Allow the widow to keep her necessary clothing, bedding, and cooking utensils even if the estate is insolvent.

grounds.citation: Women and the Law of Property in Early America, PDF p. 250–251
grounds.quote: widows received dower in realty before lands could be attached by creditors
grounds.point: Give your widow dower in one-third of your real property before creditors may take it.

rulings.resolution: English and early American law as Ditz and Salmon report it set the widow's dower, her necessaries (bedding, clothing, cooking things) and her life share ahead of heirs AND creditors, even when the estate was insolvent. The duty puts all debts before any inheritance, which would let creditors take what the widow is owed.
rulings.revision: Pay the funeral charges and debts of the dead, and make good his pledges, before anyone takes an inheritance; but first set apart his widow's dower and necessaries, which no creditor may take.

rulings.topic: See that every funeral has a chief mourner: the nearest senior man of the house presides and receives the mourners.
rulings.question: The newly read books show the wording of this duty (Confucian · Liji, Za Ji II.i.39–II.ii.15).
rulings.practice: See that every funeral has a chief mourner: the nearest senior man of the house presides and receives the mourners.

grounds.citation: Chu Hsi's Family Rituals, Glossary
grounds.quote: presiding mourner (generally the eldest son)
grounds.point: Serve as presiding mourner at your parent's funeral.

grounds.citation: Mourning in Late Imperial China, PDF pp. 57-58
grounds.quote: A grandson would serve as chief mourner when his father predeceased his grandfather.
grounds.point: When your father died before your grandfather, serve as chief mourner at your grandfather's death and hasten home.

grounds.citation: Mourning in Late Imperial China, PDF p. 152–153
grounds.quote: the eldest son played such an important role at the funeral
grounds.point: Lead the funeral rituals for your parents.

grounds.citation: Mourning in Late Imperial China, PDF p. 152–153
grounds.quote: his duties would be performed by the eldest grandson
grounds.point: If your father, the eldest son, has died before your grandfather, lead the funeral rituals in his place.

grounds.citation: Mourning in Late Imperial China, p. 139
grounds.quote: mourning great-grandparents, provided he was the eldest great-grandson, and the eldest son and grandson had predeceased him.
grounds.point: If you are the eldest great-grandson and the eldest son and grandson have predeceased you, take mourning for your great-grandparents.

grounds.citation: Ancestor Worship and Korean Society, Becoming an Ancestor 63-64
grounds.quote: the eldest son of the deceased, is the quintessential mourner and is responsible for the conduct of the funeral.
grounds.point: Take charge of your parent's funeral as chief mourner, responsible for its proper conduct, and hold the head of the corpse while it is dressed.

rulings.resolution: Chu Hsi's Family Rituals and the studies of Chinese and Korean mourning name the eldest son of the dead as presiding mourner, and the eldest grandson when his father died first; 'the nearest senior man of the house' could give the role to an uncle or elder cousin over the son. Mourning in Late Imperial China: when the eldest son has died before his father, the eldest grandson (or great-grandson) takes his place as chief mourner. Headship of the funeral passes down the senior line by representation, not simply to the nearest senior man such as an uncle.
rulings.revision: See that every funeral has a chief mourner: the eldest son of the dead presides and receives the mourners, or his own eldest son in his place if he has died; failing both, the nearest senior man of the house.

rulings.topic: Take into the house only those who fear God and whom you can govern.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Puritan · Christian Directory, Part II: Christian Oeconomicks, Chapter 2, Part 1).
rulings.practice: Take into the house only those who fear God and whom you can govern.

held_by.citation: Christian Directory, Part II: Christian Oeconomicks, Chapter 2, Part 1

grounds.citation: Christian Behaviour, 2. Believers be Careful that Works are Good
grounds.quote: First, if possibly they can, to get them that fear God.
grounds.point: If possible, get servants who fear God.

grounds.citation: Christian Behaviour, 2. Believers be Careful that Works are Good
grounds.quote: deal with him, as to admonition, as with thy children. Given him the same bread of God thou givest to them
grounds.point: If you have to hire unbelievers, deal with them as with children in admonition and give them the same spiritual food, seeking their good in body and soul.

rulings.resolution: Bunyan says to get servants who fear God 'if possibly they can', and if unbelievers must be hired, to admonish them as one's own children and give them the same spiritual food. The duty's 'only' is stricter than the source.
rulings.revision: Take into the house, where you can, servants who fear God and whom you can govern; if you must take others, bring them under the same teaching and admonition as your own children.

rulings.topic: Do not favor one child over another: deal fairly and evenly with all, sons and daughters, in daily care and in dividing the inheritance.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Puritan · A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, A GODLY FORME OF HOVSHOLD GOVERNMENT: CAREFVLLY TO be practised of all Christian Housholders.).
rulings.practice: Do not favor one child over another: deal fairly and evenly with all, sons and daughters, in daily care and in dividing the inheritance.

held_by.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, A GODLY FORME OF HOVSHOLD GOVERNMENT: CAREFVLLY TO be practised of all Christian Housholders.

grounds.citation: Family and Inheritance, Inheritance and settlement by great landowners
grounds.quote: entails were used to set up rules of succession for great families... their common characteristic was that they changed or suspended the rules of customary law, especially those concerning the rights of younger children.
grounds.point: Set a rule of succession that gives preference to your eldest son and suspends the usual rights of younger children.

grounds.citation: Family and Inheritance, p. 278
grounds.quote: settled as much as possible of their property intact for the eldest son, while leaving the other children their legitim
grounds.point: Settle as much of your property as possible intact on your eldest son, to preserve the splendour and dignity of the house.

grounds.citation: English Villagers of the Thirteenth Century, PDF p. 145-147
grounds.quote: A family holding, villagers felt, was not to be diminished by alienation
grounds.point: Do not diminish the family holding by alienation; keep it constant from generation to generation.

grounds.citation: Land, Kinship and Life-Cycle, PDF p. 339
grounds.quote: house and land were involved these usually went to the eldest son, the other child or children receiving cash or goods
grounds.point: If you have two or more sons, give your house and land to your eldest son unless he is already married and established, in which case give it to a younger child; provide cash or goods for your other children.

grounds.citation: Land, Kinship and Life-Cycle, PDF p. 339
grounds.quote: Land and house usually went to the son. An additional house or houses might go to the daughters. Cash and goods were divided among children
grounds.point: If you have an only son and daughters, give your house and land to your son, provide houses for your daughters as you can, and divide your money and goods among your children without gross inequality.

grounds.citation: Family and Inheritance: Rural Society in Western Europe, 1200-1800, PDF p. 404 … PDF p. 405
grounds.quote: to the exclusion, except for their dowries, of daughters
grounds.point: Give your daughters dowries, but do not give them an inheritance share.

grounds.citation: Family and Inheritance, pp. 400-401
grounds.quote: a son’s share was double that of a daughter
grounds.point: Give each daughter half the share of a son in your inheritance.

grounds.citation: Family and Inheritance, pp. 62-63
grounds.quote: daughters are not allowed to inherit, only sons... they rest content with a pittance as their share.
grounds.point: In Normandy, leave your estate only to your sons, dividing it equally among them; give your daughters only a pittance.

rulings.resolution: English entails and New England law gave the eldest son a preferred or double share (cf. Deut 21:17, already duty 159); 'evenly' in dividing the inheritance contradicts the firstborn's portion. The inheritance scholarship (Ditz, Shammas, Homans, Stone, Spufford, Deuchler and others) shows English, colonial and Korean fathers commonly kept the land or homestead whole for one son, often the eldest. The other children, daughters especially, got portions in money, goods or a trade, often smaller ones; New England intestacy gave the eldest a double share. Duty 368 reads as a demand for equal division, which these sources do not support. Fairness in their sense means a just portion for every child, not equal shares. Korean, French and many New England customs divided every asset equally, but English, New England and Korean sources often pass the land or house whole to one heir (in Scripture the firstborn has a double portion, see [159]) and make up the others' portions in cash or goods. 'Evenly ... in dividing the inheritance' reads as equal division of every asset and sits uneasily with [159].
rulings.revision: Do not favor one child over another: deal fairly with all, sons and daughters, in daily care and in providing for each; where the land or house must pass whole to one heir, or the firstborn takes his due, make up the others' portions in money or goods.

rulings.topic: Guard each other's good name: cover each other's failings, do not believe light reports against each other, and defend each other from slander.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Puritan · A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife).
rulings.practice: Guard each other's good name: cover each other's failings, do not believe light reports against each other, and defend each other from slander.

held_by.citation: A Godly Forme of Houshold Government, 1. The dutie of the Husband towards his Wife

grounds.citation: Richard Steele, in The Godly Home, Section 3
grounds.quote: Faithfulness also involves keeping each other’s secrets. These must not be disclosed unless there is a greater obligation.
grounds.point: Do not disclose your spouse's secrets unless a greater obligation requires it.

grounds.citation: Richard Steele, in Una teología de la familia, Los deberes de esposos y esposas
grounds.quote: La fidelidad también incluye guardar los secretos del otro. Estos no deben revelarse, a menos que exista una obligación mayor.
grounds.point: Keep one another's secrets and do not reveal them unless a greater obligation requires.

rulings.resolution: Puritan and Modern Reformed sources (Godly Home; Una teología de la familia) say spouses must keep each other's secrets 'unless a greater obligation requires' disclosure; the duty to cover failings omits that limit.
rulings.revision: Guard each other's good name: cover each other's failings and keep each other's secrets unless a greater duty requires otherwise, do not believe light reports against each other, and defend each other from slander.

rulings.topic: Hold your dower in trust for the heir: keep it in good repair, do not waste or sell it, and deal honestly with him.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (English custom · Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · IV.).
rulings.practice: Hold your dower in trust for the heir: keep it in good repair, do not waste or sell it, and deal honestly with him.

held_by.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · IV.

grounds.citation: Family and Inheritance, PDF p. 175–176
grounds.quote: for 21 years until his child came of age.
grounds.point: Hold the land left to you for your child until he comes of age, then pass it to him.

grounds.citation: English Villagers of the Thirteenth Century, p. 204
grounds.quote: a widow lost all or a part of the free bench which she held after her husband's death when the heir of the tenement... came of age
grounds.point: When the heir comes of age, give up the free bench you hold from your husband.

grounds.citation: English Villagers, 180-181
grounds.quote: then widows ought to surrender to the younger son, as heir, a moiety of the inheritance.
grounds.point: When your husband's younger son comes of age, surrender to him as heir a moiety of the inheritance, keeping only your bench.

grounds.citation: English Villagers of the Thirteenth Century, p. 454 n. 4
grounds.quote: vidue reddere debent filio iuniori v t heredi medietatem hereditatis — widows ought to return to the younger son as heir half of the inheritance.
grounds.point: When your son comes of age at fifteen, give him half of the inheritance.

grounds.citation: Homans, English Villagers of the Thirteenth Century, Ch. IX n.8
grounds.quote: Helewysa que fuit vxor Roberti le Capel venit in plena curia et reddit sursum domino .ij. partes tocius tenementi
grounds.point: Give up the two parts of your late husband's land to his son, keeping only your own portion.

grounds.citation: English Villagers of the Thirteenth Century, Impartible Inheritance of Land
grounds.quote: the custom was that the widow held all of her late husband's tenement until her youngest son, the heir of the tenement, was fifteen years of age.
grounds.point: Hold your late husband's tenement for your youngest son until he is fifteen, then surrender it except for your widow's bench.

grounds.citation: Goody, Family and Inheritance, p. 35
grounds.quote: she held all her late husband’s tenement until her youngest son reached the age of fifteen
grounds.point: Hold your late husband's tenement until the youngest son reaches fifteen; shield him and the holding.

grounds.citation: English Villagers, 180-181
grounds.quote: She might not permanently alienate it.
grounds.point: Do not permanently alienate your bench; at your death it must revert to the holder of the rest of the tenement.

rulings.resolution: English manorial custom, colonial law and Korean law all add that the widow holds the heir's land only until he comes of age, then surrenders it (keeping her bench or dower), and that the dower itself reverts to the heirs at her death; she may not alienate it permanently.
rulings.revision: Hold your dower and what you keep of his father's estate in trust for the heir: keep it in good repair, do not waste, sell or give it away, hand over his holding when he comes of age, and let your dower pass to him at your death.

rulings.topic: When her husband is absent, disabled, negligent or dead, take up the ordering of the house and its worship in his place.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Puritan · Christian Directory, Part II, Chapter 9, Direct. 11).
rulings.practice: When her husband is absent, disabled, negligent or dead, take up the ordering of the house and its worship in his place.

held_by.citation: Christian Directory, Part II, Chapter 9, Direct. 11

grounds.citation: William S. Plumer, in Una teología de la familia, 13
grounds.quote: Le corresponde reunir a sus hijos y sirvientes en un lugar apropiado y enseñarles, sumándose a ellos en actos adecuados de devoción. — It is her place to gather her children and servants in an appropriate place and teach them, joining them in appropriate acts of devotion.
grounds.point: When your husband neglects family worship, gather your children and servants and teach them, under his authority.

grounds.citation: James W. Alexander, in Una teología de la familia, La adoración familiar dirigida por mujeres
grounds.quote: deberá seguir el ejemplo de Ester... con sus criadas y los niños más pequeños cumpliendo con esta adoración
grounds.point: If no man in the household is willing or fit to lead worship, gather the women and children and lead them yourself, and earnestly urge the rest not to omit daily prayer.

grounds.citation: Richard Steele, in Una teología de la familia, 'El respeto de la esposa por su esposo'
grounds.quote: deber de la esposa sujetarse a su esposo como su cabeza, (excepto en casos en que la cabeza esté demente o evidencie un desorden mental)
grounds.point: Subject yourself to him as your head, except if he is demented or mentally disordered.

grounds.citation: Arthur W. Pink, in Una teología de la familia, Culto familiar
grounds.quote: pero si está ausente o gravemente enfermo, o es inconverso, entonces la esposa tomará su lugar. — but if he is absent or gravely ill, or unconverted, then the wife will take his place.
grounds.point: If the head of the household is absent, seriously ill, or unconverted, take his place and lead the family worship.

grounds.citation: Arthur W. Pink, in The Godly Home, Section 2
grounds.quote: if he be absent, or seriously ill, or an unbeliever, then the wife would take his place
grounds.point: If the head of the house is absent, seriously ill, or an unbeliever, take his place and lead the family devotions.

rulings.resolution: Bunyan-era and modern Reformed sources give the wife the lead of the house and its worship when the husband is absent, gravely ill, dead, insane or unconverted, or when no man is fit. Where he is merely negligent, they have her remind and urge him and teach the children and servants under his authority (Yuan Ts'ai likewise: manage for a dull husband without exceeding her place). The duty's word 'negligent' lets her displace him; it also omits the unbelieving husband.
rulings.revision: When her husband is absent, gravely ill, dead or an unbeliever, take up the ordering of the house and its worship in his place; where he is only negligent, urge him to it and meanwhile teach the children and servants under his authority, not over him.

rulings.topic: In your wife's family's own affairs, the decision belongs to her father and his house: you are of another house, so do not meddle; give counsel when it is asked.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Scripture · Prov 26:17).
rulings.practice: In your wife's family's own affairs, the decision belongs to her father and his house: you are of another house, so do not meddle; give counsel when it is asked.

grounds.citation: Those Who Stayed Behind, pp. 118-119
grounds.quote: Scales eventually carried on the farm and cared for him in his retirement.
grounds.point: Care for your wife's father in his old age, especially if he has no son to carry on the farm.

grounds.citation: The Confucian Transformation of Korea, PDF p. 82-83
grounds.quote: a son-in-law (so, yoso) took the place of a son in a household that lacked a male heir.
grounds.point: Take the place of a son in your wife's household when it has no male heir.

grounds.citation: Under the Ancestors' Eyes, PDF p. 119
grounds.quote: Because Chip-kyŏng did not have a son, Yu-on became his heir and thus established the Sunch’ŏn Kim in the Andong area.
grounds.point: If your wife's father has no son, become his heir and continue his line.

grounds.citation: Ancestor Worship and Korean Society, Ancestor Cults in East Asia Compared
grounds.quote: later assigns his wife’s natal surname to one or more of his offspring
grounds.point: When you marry into your wife’s home, give at least one of your children her family’s surname to continue her line.

rulings.resolution: Where the wife's father had no son, the son-in-law took a son's place in that house. In New England he carried on the farm and cared for him in retirement (Barron). In Korea he took the place of a son or heir (Deuchler, Janelli). The duty treats him as always of another house, which leaves no room for this, and it already sits uneasily with seed 59 ('be a son to his wife's parents, not a guest').
rulings.revision: In your wife's family's own affairs, the decision belongs to her father and his house: you are of another house, so do not meddle, and give counsel when it is asked. But where her father has no son, stand in a son's place for him: take up the work he cannot carry and care for him in age.

rulings.topic: When the family judges a member's fault, or whether to cut one off, hear the matter through and let your elders speak first; then say plainly what you know to be true and right, and do not keep silent while one is wronged.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Scripture · Job 32:4-10).
rulings.practice: When the family judges a member's fault, or whether to cut one off, hear the matter through and let your elders speak first; then say plainly what you know to be true and right, and do not keep silent while one is wronged.

grounds.citation: Lineage Organization in Southeastern China, PDF pp. 111-113
grounds.quote: the rule of no intervention in one another's concerns
grounds.point: Do not intervene in the concerns of your child's spouse's parents.

rulings.resolution: Freedman reports a rule of no intervention between houses joined by marriage in each other's concerns. The duty seats the son-in-law in his wife's family's judgment, with a voice after the elders, a standing no source gives him. The duty's last clause (speak the truth; do not keep silent while one is wronged) is uncontradicted, but his part should be a witness's or a counselor's, not a judge's, which also fits seed 431.
rulings.revision: When your wife's family judges a member's fault, or whether to cut one off, the judgment is theirs, not yours: if you are asked, or if you know facts the matter turns on, say plainly what is true, and do not keep silent while one is wronged; otherwise hold your peace.

rulings.topic: When the family judges a member's fault, or whether to cut one off, hear the matter through and let your elders speak first; then say plainly what you know to be true and right, and do not keep silent while one is wronged.
rulings.question: The newly read books qualify this duty (Scripture · Job 32:4-10).
rulings.practice: When the family judges a member's fault, or whether to cut one off, hear the matter through and let your elders speak first; then say plainly what you know to be true and right, and do not keep silent while one is wronged.

grounds.citation: Yüan Ts'ai, Precepts 1.5
grounds.quote: they may not consider themselves peers who may dispute points whenever they please
grounds.point: Consider the needs and feelings of your elder brother, and do not consider yourself a peer who may dispute points whenever you please.

grounds.citation: Yüan Ts'ai, Precepts 1.5
grounds.quote: a younger brother to his elder brother is like that of a soldier to his officer... they may not consider themselves peers who may dispute points whenever they please.
grounds.point: Do not treat yourself as your elder brother's peer; when he is remiss, suggest tactfully, and if he insists, listen submissively and do not argue.

grounds.citation: Lineage Organization in Southeastern China, PDF pp. 111-113
grounds.quote: Her own family had no clearly defined right to interfere in her affairs once she had gone out in marriage
grounds.point: Do not interfere in the affairs of your married-out daughter or sister.

rulings.resolution: Yuan Ts'ai: a younger brother may not treat his elder as a peer who disputes whenever he pleases; when the elder is remiss he suggests it tactfully, and if the elder insists he listens without arguing. This applies here because seed 430 gives the elder brother-in-law an elder's place. Freedman: a married woman's own kin, her brothers included, had no defined right to interfere in her affairs once she married out. The duty's 'say plainly' omits both the manner (tactfully, once, without disputing) and the limit of standing. Its text is also identical to seed 432's, though the two role pairs differ.
rulings.revision: When the family judges a member's fault, or whether to cut one off, hear the matter through and let your elders speak first; then say respectfully and plainly what you know to be true, and do not keep silent while one is wronged; but do not dispute with your elder brother-in-law as an equal, and where the judgment belongs to his house and not yours, leave it there.

rulings.topic: Serve them by the proper forms while they live; bury and remember them by the proper forms when they die.
rulings.question: The newly read books show the wording of this duty (Confucian · Analects 2:5).
rulings.practice: Serve them by the proper forms while they live; bury and remember them by the proper forms when they die.

grounds.citation: Mencius 3A.2 (Legge)
grounds.quote: When parents are alive, they should be served according to propriety; when they are dead, they should be buried according to propriety; and they should be sacrificed to according to propriety
grounds.point: The passage the duty cites goes on to sacrifice, which the duty rendered as 'remember'.

grounds.citation: Mencius 3A.2
grounds.quote: 生，事之以禮；死，葬之以禮，祭之以禮
grounds.point: 祭 is sacrifice, not remembrance.

rulings.resolution: The duty renders Analects 2:5 as 'bury and remember them', but the text says sacrifice (祭之以禮), as Mencius 3A.2 quotes it. The duty softened a rite the house does not keep (see 247) into remembrance. Keep the true reading for the living and the burial, and leave the sacrifice out.
rulings.revision: Serve your parents by the proper forms while they live, and bury them by the proper forms when they die.

rulings.topic: Pray for the dead of the family.
rulings.question: The newly read books contradict this duty (Catholic · CCC 958, 1032).
rulings.practice: Pray for the dead of the family.

grounds.citation: WCF 21.4
grounds.quote: Prayer is to be made for things lawful, and for all sorts of men living, or that shall live hereafter: but, not for the Dead
grounds.point: Westminster forbids prayer for the dead.

grounds.citation: WLC 183
grounds.quote: but not for the dead
grounds.point: The Larger Catechism says the same.

grounds.citation: 2 Samuel 12:23
grounds.quote: But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast? can I bring him back again?
grounds.point: David stopped his fasting and prayer when the child died.

rulings.resolution: A Catholic duty to pray for the dead sits on the list as a live draft. Westminster forbids it in so many words, and David ceased to pray once the child had died. It belongs with the rites the house does not keep.
